title: Could Marvin Harrison Jr. become a Colts trade target?
summary: Marvin Harrison Jr. to Indianapolis sounds like fan fiction the first time you say it, mostly because of the last name on the jersey. The Colts drafting or trading for Marvin Harrison’s son would be one of those stories that feels almost too neat, the kind of full-circle reunion that writes itself before you even […]
full_text: GLENDALE, ARIZONA - JULY 26: Marvin Harrison Jr. #18 of the Arizona Cardinals participates in a team practice ahead of the NFL season at State Farm Stadium on July 26, 2026 in Glendale, Arizona. (Photo by Christian Petersen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Marvin Harrison Jr. to Indianapolis sounds like fan fiction the first time you say it, mostly because of the last name on the jersey. The Colts drafting or trading for Marvin Harrison’s son would be one of those stories that feels almost too neat, the kind of full-circle reunion that writes itself before you even get to the football part. The connection is obvious. Marvin Harrison Sr. is one of the greatest players in Colts history and one of the best receivers to ever play the position. His son wearing that same horseshoe would be an easy story to sell. Harrison’s start in Arizona has not gone the way many expected. His second season was described by many Cardinals analysts as “incomplete” and “unfortunate,” and the production matched that sentiment: 41 catches, 608 yards and four touchdowns, finishing behind Trey McBride and Michael Wilson in the passing game. Wilson, meanwhile, broke out for over 1,000 yards and has kept building momentum as a major piece of Arizona’s offense. That does not mean the Cards are shopping Harrison, and it does not mean they should be in a rush to do it. He was the No. 4 pick in 2024, he had elite college production, and the traits that made him one of the safest receiver prospects in recent memory did not just disappear. Teams do not usually give up on that kind of player quickly, especially when the cheaper and more logical answer is to try to fix it first. If the situation keeps trending in the wrong direction, though, the Colts should be paying attention. The Cardinals may have a big decision coming The Cardinals drafted Harrison to become their No. 1 receiver, and that door is not closed. The talent is still there. The size, body control, pedigree and route-running foundation did not vanish after two uneven seasons, which is why Arizona is far more likely to keep trying to fix the situation than admit defeat this early. The problem is that the NFL does not usually wait around forever, especially when other players start taking the role you were supposed to own. Wilson’s emergence is big, and McBride is already one of the best tight ends in football and a major piece of the passing game. If Wilson is becoming Arizona’s top outside presence while Harrison continues to look unsure, banged up, inconsistent or low on confidence, then at some point the Cardinals have to ask what his role actually is. His value is not what it was on draft night, because it can’t be. A former top-five pick who has not produced like a top-five pick does not carry the same value he had before playing an NFL snap. Arizona may still view him as part of its future, but if his role keeps shrinking and the confidence does not come back, there is at least a scenario where a reset starts making sense for both sides. The Colts should be ready if that scenario ever becomes real. The fit in Indianapolis is clear The Colts also have a real need at receiver, which is what makes this more than a fun last-name story. Michael Pittman Jr. is gone after being traded to Pittsburgh, leaving the receiver room in a different place. Alec Pierce is still the vertical outside threat, Josh Downs is the slot, and Tyler Warren is entering his second season as a major weapon at tight end. That is not a bad group, but it is missing a clean Pittman replacement at Z receiver, and that is exactly where Harrison could fit. He would not have to come in and be a finished superstar on Day 1. The appeal is that he gives the Colts a young outside receiver with WR1 traits, even if he has not become that player yet. Indianapolis does not just need another body in the receiver room. It needs someone with the talent to grow into a top target, win outside, draw coverage and become part of the long-term core no matter who is playing quarterback. That is why Harrison is so appealing as this would not be a nostalgia trade, even though the family connection would make the story louder and probably make Indianapolis more attractive if Harrison ever wanted a fresh start. The football case is strong enough on its own. The Colts need a young outside receiver with high-end talent, and Harrison may eventually need a place where his confidence, role and development can reset. The price should not be a first-round pick There is a reason Arizona would hesitate, and there is also a reason the Colts would need to be careful. Harrison has not proven he is a star yet, which is the entire reason this conversation exists in the first place. Trading for him would mean betting on talent, pedigree and fit more than proven NFL production, and that type of bet can absolutely go wrong. A change of scenery can unlock a player, but it can also expose that the problems were bigger than the situation. The confidence piece is probably the most important part. If Harrison is struggling because the role has been messy, the quarterback fit has been inconsistent, or Arizona has not found the right way to feature him, then the Colts should be interested. If the issue is that the separation, physicality and reliability are not translating cleanly to the NFL, then the risk becomes much harder to ignore. That is why this should be viewed as a situation to monitor, not a move to force at any cost. The Colts should not act desperate, and they should not pay like they are acquiring a proven top-10 receiver. Harrison should be viewed as a distressed, high-upside asset, which is exactly the kind of player worth checking on when a team has a clear need and the price may be lower than the name suggests. Why the Colts should be aggressive if Arizona listens The Colts have spent too many years patching holes instead of attacking them, and receiver is one of the spots where that approach has shown up. Pierce has value, Downs is a good player, and Warren could become a special weapon at tight end, but that still does not give Indianapolis the long-term outside receiver group it needs. The Colts traded Pittman, and while they have pieces, they do not have a clear replacement with the size, pedigree and upside to grow into that role. That is what makes Harrison worth the swing. A 2027 second-round pick is not nothing, but it should not scare the Colts away from adding a young receiver with this kind of talent at a clear position of need. The best version of Harrison in Indianapolis is easy to see: he steps into the Pittman role, Pierce keeps stretching the field, Downs works inside, Warren becomes the matchup problem at tight end, and the offense suddenly has a much more balanced group of weapons. That kind of receiver room would make life easier for Daniel Jones now and for whoever leads the offense beyond him. The family connection only adds to the appeal. There would be pressure, obviously, because playing in the same city where his father became a legend would not be simple. There could also be comfort in it, though. Indianapolis would embrace him quickly, the organization understands what the Harrison name means, and the move would give him a fresh start with a franchise that has every reason to want it to work. Final thought The Colts should call if Marvin Harrison Jr.’s situation in Arizona keeps slipping, even if that does not mean the Cardinals are anywhere close to trading him right now. They probably are not. A former No. 4 pick with that kind of talent is not the type of player teams move quickly, and Arizona’s first choice will almost certainly be to rebuild his confidence, settle his role and make the Wilson-Harrison-McBride trio work. Indianapolis should still be paying attention. If Wilson continues taking over as Arizona’s top receiver, Harrison’s role keeps shrinking, or the Cardinals eventually decide a reset is better than forcing the fit, the Colts should be…

Top 10 Quarterbacks In Summer Scouting Dante Moore, Oregon*: Round 1 Grade Arch Manning, Texas*: Round 1 Grade Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State*: Round 1-2 Grade CJ Carr, Notre Dame*: Round 1-2 Grade Julian Sayin, Ohio State*: Round 1-2 Grade Darian Mensah, Miami*: Round 1-2 Grade Jayden Maiava, USC: Round 2 Grade Drake Lindsey, Minnesota*: Round 2 Grade Trinidad Chambliss, Ole Miss: Round 2-3 Grade LaNorris Sellers, South Carolina*: Round 3 Grade Honorable Mentions Josh Hoover, Indiana Sam Leavitt, LSU* Brenden Sorsby, n/a Katin Houser, Illinois John Mateer, Oklahoma *Has remaining eligibility post-2026 collegiate season. All we've heard for the last year is how legendary the 2027 quarterback class is. Today it's time to find out SUMMER SCOUTING IS BACK @ConnorJRogers & I are live on @NFLSEshow right now giving you our top 12 QBs for the 2027 NFL Draft Come hangout! https://t.co/NrbppfLBgu — Trevor Sikkema (@TampaBayTre) June 22, 2026 Tier 1: Definitely Outside Colts Pick Range Dante Moore really impressed me throughout the 2025 season, raising his stock significantly as the year went on. He will be missing his top target Kenyon Sadiq from last year, but the Ducks have a strong successor in Jamari Johnson who could be another Round 1 Tight End in the 2027 Draft. The WR2 of 2024 behind Tez Johnson returns with Evan Stewart coming back from injury that cost him all of 2025. They also added a speedy slot Iverson Hooks out of UAB to the room. Dante Moore | QB | Oregon | 6-3, 215 Natural in every way of playing the position. Smooth release that distributes in a timely and efficient manner. Plays with his eyes, feet, and motion all connected. pic.twitter.com/oCTwZdcAZ3 — Jordan Reid (@Jordan_Reid) June 26, 2026 Can Moore build off of his impressive 2025 season? Can he step up after draft losses to his offensive line and top target? Was the issues against the Hoosiers’ pressure a sign of his limits as a passer or just a rare off game or two? Can he show off more dynamism as a mobile QB and increase his decent but nothing special ball velocity? Arch Manning is the continuation of the Manning Quarterback dynasty. The nephew of both Peyton and Eli and grandson of Archie, he inherited his dad Cooper’s athleticism as the only Manning who didn’t play QB: he was a highly recruited wideout. So unlike his uncles and grandfather, Arch can run like a dual threat QB with 399 yards and 10 Rush TDs in his first year as a starter at Texas. Quick scouting reports on some of the top QBs that could be in the 2027 NFL draft: • Arch Manning, Texas • Dante Moore, Oregon • CJ Carr, Notre Dame • Drew Mestemaker, Oklahoma State • Darian Mensah, Miami pic.twitter.com/jeuxKUcHm7 — Jordan Reid (@Jordan_Reid) July 15, 2026 He still had his inconsistencies on tape, especially early on in 2025. But there were flashes of true dominance and high end QB talent worthy of his family’s legacy. He knows what to do in terms of processing, field reading, passing technique, and touch. Manning just needs to show it more consistently and be more disciplined. With Arch’s tantalizing upside and resources to at least 1 Hall of Fame QB (and 2 Hall of Very Good QBs at worst on top of that), there is a strong chance he continues the family legacy of being a top draft pick. After all, the lowest draft pick in the Manning family is his grandfather Archie at 2nd Overall. Arch could very well be the QB1 on my board once the season begins, but based off of 2025 tape I got Dante Moore just ahead of him due to more consistent tape of Moore being a very polished QB. Deep Class…maybe Much has been said about the depth of the 2027 QB draft class. This class has a lot of hype behind it, but plenty of questions remain for all these QBs. 2026 will be a big opportunity for each of these passers to show development and vie for positioning on the QB totem pole. Only two currently have Round 1 Grades for me, but that can change and QBflation in draft big boards vs draft slot is a major thing. There could be a lot of jostling and changes in rankings by end of season. One under-reported factor that dilutes the hype of this QB class: 8 of the Top 10 QBs in the class has remaining eligibility left. With NIL contracts getting more and more lucrative, plenty of QBs have opted to stay longer in college in recent years to continue to develop/try to improve their draft stock rather than enter the NFL Draft immediately. Dante Moore most notably could have competed with Fernando Mendoza for the top QB in the 2026 Draft and was a lock to go in the top 5 of the draft, but opted to return to Oregon. ✍️ Why is Dante Moore still here? Instead of being a New York Jet with $50 million guaranteed, he's still Oregon's QB. Why he came back and why he says it wasn't about the Jets. "He didn’t want to let $50 million get in the way of $600 million." Story: https://t.co/AV2oDXv5Tc pic.twitter.com/9jW5u00UIr — Chris Vannini (@ChrisVannini) July 28, 2026 There is hardly a guarantee even half of the QBs listed in the top 10 enter the 2027 Draft, and even then the 5 that do could very well get taken before the Colts Round 2 pick. The Colts will be hoping for a large amount of declares if they decide they need to address QB in 2027, as otherwise their options may be amongst the honorable mention QBs. Or they could hope for a lot of QBs to return to college and potentially boost the 2028 Draft class when the Colts have their own Round 1 pick back again. The Best Last Year Eligibility QBs Of the QBs with no eligibility left after 2026, Jayden Maiava from USC and Trinidad Chambliss out of Ole Miss stand out as the top 2, with Indiana’s Josh Hoover and Illinois Katin Houser up transferring to the BIG10 and having opportunities to really raise their stock against one of the toughest conferences in college after previous starting experiences at TCU for Hoover and Michigan State (freshman year) and East Carolina for Houser. Maiava is a prototypical size QB at 6’4 230 lbs and has showcased a ton of toughness, escapability as an improviser, high end velocity, and touch passes into tight windows at every depth. He had some spectacular throws on tape to Makai Lemon and Ja’Kobi Lane, helping both of them be very productive and well drafted in 2026. Jayden Maiava 2025 pic.twitter.com/j4QRubE70F — James Foster (@NoFlagsFilm) July 16, 2026 The native Hawaiian also has shown strong presnap adjustments and identification, able to find soft spots in coverage and mismatches consistently. His problems predominantly lie with his gunslinger mentality, which has gotten him in trouble (26 INTs in 34 games) with picks. Paired with some questionable field reading post snap and inconsistent mechanics in his throwing platform that cause inaccuracy at times, Maiava still has work to do to reach his potential. title: Chiefs training camp notebook Day 4: Defense is challenging Mahomes
summary: For the fourth consecutive day in St. Joe, Kansas City Chiefs players, coaches and fans were treated to a cool morning; this practice was breezy but sunny, and lasted roughly two hours. The team is looking ahead to a rest day on Sunday before the pads come on Monday. Here’s everything to know from Arrowhead […]
full_text: ST. JOSEPH, MO - JULY 29: Drue Tranquill #23 walks to the field before practice during the Kansas City Chiefs training camp on July 29, 2026 at Missouri Western State University in St. Joseph, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images For the fourth consecutive day in St. Joe, Kansas City Chiefs players, coaches and fans were treated to a cool morning; this practice was breezy but sunny, and lasted roughly two hours. The team is looking ahead to a rest day on Sunday before the pads come on Monday. Here’s everything to know from Arrowhead Pride’s in-person observations of Saturday’s practice: Injury update Jared Sapp has the details on rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allen’s mid-practice injury that drew a loud gasp from the crowd watching. It happened during punt team. Dave Toub on Cyrus Allen: “I hate to see somebody get hurt, especially on special teams. He’s doing well on offense & for me, too. He’s was a gunner & a returner. Everyone is on special teams until they aren’t. Everyone starts as a 4-phase guy, especially rookies.” — Nate Taylor (@ByNateTaylor) August 1, 2026 Defensive lineup notes With defensive end Ashton Gillotte unavailable due to a strained hamstring he suffered during Friday’s practice, fourth-year player Felix Anudike-Uzomah stepped up to play more with the starting defense on Saturday. As practice began, the first-team unit walked through different formations. Most notable was this year’s first look at Dime personnel, the defensive formation with six defensive backs, one linebacker and four pass-rushing threats up front. In the back end, cornerbacks Mansoor Delane and Nohl Williams manned the outside spots. Safety Christian Roland-Wallace stayed as the slot defender, the same role he mans in Nickel formations, and L’Jarius Sneed was substituted in the place of second linebacker Drue Tranquill coming off the field. Through the first three days of camp, it appeared Sneed — who still leaves practice early for planned rehabilitation — was preparing to play on the outside. However, this suggests defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo is, at the very least, considering using Sneed as the Dime safety. Against a balanced set, this would set up Sneed and Roland-Wallace as the two slot defenders to take on slot receivers, tight ends and running backs on pass downs. Up front, the Chiefs teased a pass-rush front that had defensive ends George Karlaftis and rookie R Mason Thomas on the edge; Chris Jones and Anudike-Uzomah were rushing from inside for a look. As the practice moved forward, the Chiefs’ defense showed off multiple fronts in team periods. To start one full-team period against the starting offense, nose tackle Khyiris Tonga was joined by rookie Peter Woods on the interior instead of starter Chris Jones. Later in the period, Spagnuolo deployed a three-man front that used Tranquill as the fourth “on-ball” player along with Jones, Woods and Karlaftis. Behind them, linebackers Nick Bolton and Jeffrey Bassa played the second level in the 3-3 formation. It’s also worth pointing out that veteran linebacker Jack Cochrane appeared to rotate in with Cooper McDonald as the SAM linebacker in base formations. Offensive lineup notes The starting right tackle position continues to be manned by rookie Kahlil Benson, who appeared to be the exclusive first-team right tackle in Saturday’s practice for the third consecutive day. The second-team offensive line has featured Jaylon Moore and Esa Pole switching back and forth from right and left tackle every day. Throughout practices on Friday and Saturday, it has been clear that running back Brashard Smith has a stronger place in the Chiefs’ starting offense than rookie Emmett Johnson does. Smith played with the first-team offense during team periods early and often, catching multiple passes as an outlet in the flat for quarterback Patrick Mahomes. Lengthy pre-practice talk between Chiefs RB coach DeMarco Murray and rookie Emmett Johnson. The rook has flashed in camp, but mostly with the 2nd and 3rd teams pic.twitter.com/1i8eiNZEGG — Ron Kopp Jr (@RonOnChiefs) August 1, 2026 With Rice absent in team periods and the injury to rookie standout Cyrus Allen, the Chiefs’ starting offense featured more plays, including Nikko Remigio and Andrew Armstrong lined up at receiver. Tight ends Travis Kelce, Noah Gray and Jared Wiley are all playing a good number of snaps with Mahomes, whether the formation calls for one, two or three of them at a time. Notes from practice The Chiefs’ pass defense has not made anything easy on Mahomes during team periods or seven-on-seven work. On Friday, his receivers found more open space than previous days, but Saturday appeared to go back to closing every throwing window and making Kansas City’s pass catchers earn big plays. Wide receiver Xavier Worthy has been a prime example. We have yet to see him get easy separation in camp, aside from running past slot cornerback Kader Kohou on an all-out blitz that featured no safety help. On Saturday, Worthy overcame the tight coverage to make two finishes on two incredibly tough catches. On the first play of the initial 11-on-11 period, the Chiefs’ defense deployed a one-high safety look with man coverage. Worthy ran across the formation and looked over his shoulder for a pass with a cornerback trailing him closely and safety Alohi Gilman over the top. The pass somehow got through, and Worthy secured it in traffic. On another opening play of a full-team period, Mahomes lobbed it up for Worthy running away from man coverage to the pylon. Worthy laid out for it and secured the deep ball through the ground. On another seven-on-seven play, Gilman finished the close coverage he had over the top of a deep route by wide receiver Tyquan Thornton, burying the ball at the catch point. Gilman has given little to Mahomes over the middle, but it was Tranquill who baited him into a pick during seven-on-seven Saturday. Kelce worked a route to come open over the middle, but Tranquill read Mahomes’ eyes the whole way and jumped the pass from the backside for a highlight-reel pick. It’s clear that cornerback Mansoor Delane is playing with intensity and fire, especially after learning that he is playing one-handed during camp , potentially against the wishes of the staff. After one run play in a full-team period, he and wide receiver Nikko Remigio stayed face to face, getting into it enough for a crowd of teammates to come over and break them up to keep practice rolling. Closer to the end of practice, Delane kept his head on a swivel in zone coverage and snagged a pass off the outstretched hands of Kelce. Purposefully or not, Delane tossed the ball in Mahomes’ direction at the end of the play, symbolizing the confident mentality he has come to camp with despite donning the non-contact jersey.

title: Are the early stars of Chiefs camp emerging as future starters?
summary: It’s the most wonderful time of the year. Optimism is abound. Training camp has arrived. The possibilities for the upcoming season are endless. Everyone is looking for the next team, the next star, the next answer to a question they’ve had about their favorite team. Storylines are bound to emerge. This is the NFL, after […]
full_text: ST JOSEPH, MISSOURI - JULY 25: Cyrus Allen #13 walks toward the practice field during Kansas City Chiefs Training Camp at Missouri Western State University on July 25, 2026 in St Joseph, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images It’s the most wonderful time of the year. Optimism is abound. Training camp has arrived. The possibilities for the upcoming season are endless. Everyone is looking for the next team, the next star, the next answer to a question they’ve had about their favorite team. Storylines are bound to emerge. This is the NFL, after all. The Kansas City Chiefs are no exception to this rule. The two biggest stories early in Chiefs camp are rookie fifth-round wide receiver Cyrus Allen and undrafted offensive tackle Kahlil Benson. Both Allen and Benson are reportedly already taking some reps with quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the starting offense. That’s meaningful. The Chiefs aren’t going to waste reps, even early in camp, with the best quarterback in the game. How meaningful, though? That’s certainly up for debate. The truth is, early training camp storylines fizzle out as often as they become something legitimate. Need I remind anyone of wide receiver Justyn Ross ? How about cornerbacks Herb Miller and D’Montre Wade ? Standing out at this point in camp is objectively a positive development. It’s not guaranteed to portend future success. But sometimes it does. I was skeptical of Tyquan Thornton at this point a year ago. He made plays early and often in camp, and it ultimately translated into the regular season. He parlayed his camp breakout into a potential starting role in 2026 on a two-year contract with the Chiefs worth $11 million. Are Benson and Allen more likely to go the route of Ross, or the path of Thornton? Only time will tell. For now, let’s take a look at how each could fit into the team’s current or future plans. Kahlil Benson Benson is a heck of a project. First of all, he’s huge. He has the arm length Kansas City covets at the tackle position, and that’s a heck of a place to start. He’s also received rave reviews from coaches and teammates alike early in camp about his work ethic. A big, athletic, hard-working offensive tackle? That’s a heck of a starter pack for a potential camp surprise. Kahlil Benson is a OT prospect in the 2026 draft class. He scored a 8.84 RAS out of a possible 10.00. This ranked 191 out of 1642 OT from 1987 to 2026. https://t.co/b16NLPXBQB pic.twitter.com/1MHplATpDb — RAS.football (@MathBomb) April 11, 2026 This is where I have to pump the brakes on the hype train, at least a little bit. Benson went undrafted for a reason. There were real questions about his profile. Dane Brugler, one of the best NFL Draft analysts in the business, wrote the following about Benson in his pre-draft evaluation: “Benson has sloppy tendencies that he must continue to address, but his natural size and length — along with his run-game attitude — will give him a chance in a pro camp. His best long-term position is likely inside at guard.” Maybe Benson can out-perform those pre-draft expectations. But going from undrafted free agent to starting right tackle on a Super Bowl hopeful seems… excessively hopeful? The more likely scenario is the Chiefs like what they’ve seen from Benson and hope he can compete for a starting role as early as 2027 when the team moves on from Jaylon Moore. Such a scenario would still serve as a huge win for the Chiefs. A big piece of the puzzle on nailing late-round draft picks or undrafted free agents is the cap relief such a move can provide. Benson is signed to a 3-year contract worth a total of $3.1 million. Even his fourth year is a restricted free agent year in which the Chiefs would technically have his exclusive negotiating rights if the front office chooses to do so. Becoming a starter by year two of Benson’s NFL career would provide the Chiefs the kind of relief along the offensive line that could help to offset Creed Humphrey and Trey Smith’s cap hits. There’s an important distinction between the situation Benson finds himself in and the one Allen is inheriting. In an ideal world, the Chiefs would play the same five offensive linemen for every snap of the 2026 season. That group likely includes Josh Simmons, Kingsley Suamataia, Humphrey, Smith and Moore. The Chiefs only had two starters stay healthy the entire 2025 campaign, but those two each played 98 percent of the offensive snaps. That’s not abnormal in a typical season. Cyrus Allen That’s not true at the wide receiver position. Five different receivers played at least 300 snaps for the Chiefs last year. A rotation at the position is an accepted part of life. Different players carve out different roles, and thus playing time is easier to come by for a player like Allen, even if he isn’t installed as a true “starter.” Allen is the kind of weapon the Chiefs are lacking. His calling card is the ability to win against man coverage, something this offense could desperately use. His best reps historically have come in the slot, but smarter people than I believe he could hold his own as an option outside. If his early reps prove to be real, Allen could carve out a legitimate role within the offense. It’s unlikely he overtakes Rashee Rice, Xavier Worthy or Thornton for playing time, but could he provide the kind of value JuJu Smith-Schuster has provided as a depth option in recent years? I don’t think that’s too much to ask. A much larger role for Allen is likely to emerge in 2027 when Rice’s contract is up. It’s entirely possible the starting wide receivers next year are Worthy and Thornton with Allen in the slot, assuming this early camp breakout is real. The Chiefs might have found two under-the-radar solutions to years-long problems. That’s incredibly encouraging news in the early going of training camp. We’ll see if Allen and Benson can keep it up. For now, sit back, relax, and enjoy the ride. Football is back. What a delight.

title: Ex-Bills HC, Sean McDermott visits Rams camp
summary: Sean McDermott spent part of this year’s training camp on the West Coast, taking in practice with Sean McVay and the Los Angeles Rams. While it is common for NFL coaches to visit other organizations during the offseason or training camp, the opportunity still provides valuable insight into different coaching philosophies, practice structures, and team-building […]
full_text: Sean McDermott spent part of this year’s training camp on the West Coast, taking in practice with Sean McVay and the Los Angeles Rams. While it is common for NFL coaches to visit other organizations during the offseason or training camp, the opportunity still provides valuable insight into different coaching philosophies, practice structures, and team-building strategies. Former Bills head coach Sean McDermott is visiting today with the Los Angeles Rams. McDermott is using his off time to see how a few teams such as the Rams operate. pic.twitter.com/uWajqQuYIv — Adam Schefter (@AdamSchefter) July 31, 2026 McDermott built the Buffalo Bills into one of the AFC’s perennial contenders in a 9 year span but was let go after the 2025 season. For the Rams, welcoming an accomplished head coach such as McDermott creates an environment where ideas can be exchanged between two minds that have consistently competed at a high level over the past decade. McVay’s practices have long been praised for their organization, tempo, and efficiency. Every drill is designed with a specific purpose, and the Rams have become known for maximizing every minute of practice time. Watching those sessions firsthand gives visiting coaches a chance to evaluate new methods they may be able to incorporate into their own training camps. Those discussions can prove just as valuable as anything that happens on the field. McVay and McDermott have coached against one another several times and have developed mutual respect throughout their careers. Both entered head coaching positions in 2017 and quickly transformed their respective franchises into annual playoff contenders. While their coaching styles differ, each has established a winning culture centered around accountability and player development. McVay is widely recognized for his offensive creativity and adaptability, while McDermott has earned praise for building fundamentally sound defenses and strong locker-room leadership. Their willingness to share ideas illustrates one of the unique aspects of the NFL coaching community: competition on Sundays does not prevent collaboration throughout the offseason. The league’s best coaches are often lifelong learners, constantly searching for ways to improve every aspect of their organizations. Sean McDermott’s visit to Rams training camp naturally raises an intriguing question: could he eventually join Sean McVay’s coaching staff? While there is no indication that such a move is being discussed, McDermott would immediately become one of the NFL’s most accomplished assistant coaching candidates if he chose to return in that role. His defensive background, experience leading a playoff-caliber organization, and reputation for building disciplined teams would complement McVay’s offensive expertise. The Rams have a history of surrounding McVay with experienced football minds, making Los Angeles a logical destination if McDermott ever wanted to spend a season as a defensive coordinator or senior defensive assistant before pursuing another head coaching opportunity. Although his long-term goal is widely expected to be another head coaching position, the chance to collaborate with one of the league’s brightest offensive coaches could benefit both McDermott and the Rams.

title: Can Davante Adams do it again in 2026?
summary: Generally speaking, when a headline asks a yes or no question, the answer is “no.” It’s called Betteridge’s law of headlines, and it’s a consistent guide in the journalism world. If we apply it here, the law tells us that no, Davante Adams won’t recreate his 2025 production in 2026. OK, so it’s unlikely that […]
full_text: WOODLAND HILLS, CA - JUNE 02, 2026: Davante Adams #17 of the Los Angeles Rams runs after the catch at Rams training facility on Tuesday, June 2, 2026 in Woodland Hills, CA. (Ric Tapia / Los Angeles Times via Getty Images) Generally speaking, when a headline asks a yes or no question, the answer is “no.” It’s called Betteridge’s law of headlines, and it’s a consistent guide in the journalism world. If we apply it here, the law tells us that no, Davante Adams won’t recreate his 2025 production in 2026. OK, so it’s unlikely that Adams leads the NFL in receiving touchdowns in his age-34 season. But what can we expect from the veteran receiver? It’s not impossible, but it would be somewhat shocking to see him completely fall off a cliff. Adams’s game is built to last, as it’s based far more on technique and precision than it is on raw, physical gifts. He’s been an elite route runner with a top-tier release for the balance of his career, and it’s a career with legitimate Hall of Fame credentials . Those kinds of players generally age more gracefully at the position. Davante Adams still has the best releases in the NFL pic.twitter.com/M5pA1TOEXZ — Warren Sharp (@SharpFootball) August 1, 2026 That said, his transformation last year into the best red zone weapon in the league probably won’t continue. It could, certainly, but the odds don’t favor it. Again, he’ll turn 34 this season (albeit quite late in the year) and individual red zone production can be a volatile statistic. Even if he’s able to separate at nearly the same clip as 2025 near the goal line, there are numerous reasons why he might not score at the same level as he did a year ago. Given his age, you have to temper expectations at least somewhat, and the 2025 season is a good example why. Only six players who turned 34 or older during last season caught a pass. One of those players was Aaron Rodgers, who caught a deflection and lost nine yards. Let’s take that fluke out, leaving us with just five “skill-position” players in that age group who caught a pass in 2025. Travis Kelce: 108 targets, 76 receptions, 851 yards, 5 TD Zach Ertz: 72 targets, 50 receptions, 504 yards, 4 TD Adam Thielen: 35 targets, 19 receptions, 186 yards, 0 TD Taysom Hill: 16 targets, 11 receptions, 91 yards, 0 TD Kyle Juszczyk: 28 targets, 24 receptions, 213 yards, 2 TD That list features two tight ends, one wide receiver, one positionless offensive weapon and one fullback. That one wide receiver, the closest allegory for Adams, averaged under 10 yards per receptions, never scored and finished with a 45.7% success rate, over five percentage points below league average (per Pro-Football-Reference’s calculations. Thielen, like Adams, has always won more with route running and separation ability than physical domination, so if that’s enough to give you pause that’s understandable. But Adams will be playing his age-34 season in a far better ecosystem than either of the ones Thielen played in last season, and Adams is simply a better player than Thielen ever was. For what it’s worth, in 2024 there were also only five players in their age-34 season or older who caught a pass: Kelce, Ertz, Thielen, Hill and Marcedes Lewis (one catch, two yards). That only further hammers home that Adams is entering somewhat unchartered territory. Back to the original question. What can we actually expect from Adams in 2026? He’s WR2 in this offense behind Puka Nacua, and there isn’t a ton of depth behind him, but this offense shouldn’t require him to be an All-Pro again like he was in his late 20s. Matthew Stafford back on his BS with the no-look to Davante Adams via @Ethanshirazi24 pic.twitter.com/UtNo4VeDla — Underdog NFL (@UnderdogNFL) July 29, 2026 Nacua will see a mass quantity of targets again. The Rams have an inordinate number of tight ends in training camp and have invested both significant financial and draft capital in plenty of them, those guys will be featured heavily. And every Sean McVay team is going to run the ball plenty. When you add in all those factors, it could realistically lower Adams’s production ceiling but should also keep him from putting too much wear and tear on his body over the course of 18 weeks. Given what his role was last year, touchdowns are more important than yardage for Adams. If he racks up something in the neighborhood of the 500-700 yard range, that should be just fine. Scoring-wise, though, he hasn’t tallied fewer than eight touchdowns in seven years, and he’s scored eight or more times in nine of his 12 seasons. That seems like a reasonable goal this year, considering it’s been his baseline for the better part of a decade and he will have plenty of opportunities in this offense. Of course, that would still be somewhat unprecedented in recent memory. The last player to haul in eight or more receiving touchdowns in their age-34 season or later was Jimmy Graham in 2020 with the Chicago Bears. Prior to that? Anquan Boldin with the Detroit Lions in 2016. He was Boldin’s quarterback that season? Matthew Stafford. It’s probably not smart to expect another career season from Davante Adams in 2026. But another season in which he’s a dangerous redzone weapon and a consistent, reliable target for Stafford? That’s a much safer bet.
author: Brendan Dzwierzynski

title: Kyren Williams says Rams ‘Can’t play in the Super Bowl tomorrow’
summary: Kyren Williams joined in an interview with Kay Adams during Los Angeles Rams training camp, where Adams expressed that she was worried for the Rams because they are the favorites to win the Super Bowl. Can the team live up to those high expectations? Williams responded to Adams’s concerns with a grounded approach to the […]
full_text: LAS VEGAS, NEVADA - MAY 16: Kyren Williams arrives at the grand opening of Tailgate Beachclub at Mandalay Bay Resort And Casino on May 16, 2026 in Las Vegas, Nevada. (Photo by Denise Truscello/Getty Images for Clique Hospitality ) | Getty Images for Clique Hospital Kyren Williams joined in an interview with Kay Adams during Los Angeles Rams training camp, where Adams expressed that she was worried for the Rams because they are the favorites to win the Super Bowl. Can the team live up to those high expectations? Williams responded to Adams’s concerns with a grounded approach to the lofty prediction by expressing that none of that noise matters. Not yet. Williams even expands on his mostly grounded approach with a little philosophy. Life moves one day at a time, and that is where the Rams should focus should lie: One day at a time. Said Williams to Adams about L.A.’s projections to hoist the Lombardi Trophy this February: “None of that stuff matters right now. We’re in training camp. We can’t play the Super Bowl tomorrow. We can’t play the first game tomorrow. Only thing we an worry about is getting through today, and hopefully tomorrow, hopefully tomorrow comes…if it does then we got another chance to get better, but we’re not worried about whenever the Super Bowl is. We’re just worried about this training camp and getting better each and every single day.” Fans and talking heads can fantasize about the Super Bowl, but NFL players have to make that fantasy a reality. Williams knows his team is favored, he can simply look around the locker room and know they have some of the best talent in the NFL, but favored, not favored, who cares? What matters in the business of the NFL is who actually earns the win, not who’s favored to win. Williams is right, L.A. being favored in July/August doesn’t matter. L.A. finding a way to win the whole thing? That matters. Will the Rams live up to those high goals? Adams seems worried that it’s not likely. Williams seems focused on trying to make it happen. Like it or not, just like Williams says, the season will come one day at a time, while the Super Bowl will be played one day, whether the Rams are there or not. Tune into 2026 to watch the Rams try to carve their path one day, one game at a time.

title: An attacking Raiders defense favors safety Jeremy Chinn’s strengths
summary: A different energy and sense of urgency in training camp? Stop me if you’ve heard that before. The Las Vegas Raiders are heading in a new direction under rookie head coach Klint Kubiak. And the hackneyed phrase of new energy and sense of urgency accompanies that, of course. Acknowledged as one of the game’s top […]
full_text: Nov 30, 2025; Inglewood, California, USA; Las Vegas Raiders safety Jeremy Chinn (11) tackles Los Angeles Chargers quarterback Justin Herbert (10) during the first half at SoFi Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Jayne Kamin-Oncea-Imagn Images | Jayne Kamin-Oncea-Imagn Images A different energy and sense of urgency in training camp? Stop me if you’ve heard that before. The Las Vegas Raiders are heading in a new direction under rookie head coach Klint Kubiak. And the hackneyed phrase of new energy and sense of urgency accompanies that, of course. Acknowledged as one of the game’s top offensive minds with the play calling acumen to match the creative concoctions, it’s difficult to ignore the newness and overall excitement as the Silver & Black prep for Kubiak’s inaugural year helming a football program — his first experience of such magnitude as he heads into Year 13 in the NFL. By all accounts thus far, the Raiders coaching staff — that Kubiak assembled — is zeroed in on putting players in the best possible position to succeed. Defensive coordinator Leonard is installing an aggressive and high-energy defense that boasts a 3-4 defensive front in base formations, a departure from the four-man base fronts the Raiders deployed previously. It’s a bold maneuver by a rookie defensive play caller, but drastic measures are often dialed up to turnaround an impotent group. Leonard’s goal is to have his defense attacking the ball (reckless abandon is fine with the defensive coordinator) that minimizes hesitation and allows his defenders to relentlessly pursue and swarm ball carriers. Talk about putting players in the position to succeed. That’s not only the way Las Vegas’ elite edge rusher Maxx Crosby plays and thrives, that style of play certainly favors safety Jeremy Chinn’s strengths. By The Numbers Jeremy Chinn, Safety, 7th Year 2025: 15 games (15 starts), 114 total tackles (63 solo), 3 tackles for loss, 1 sack, 2 pass deflections, 2 forced fumbles; 996 defensive snaps Career: (2020-25), 86 games (82 starts), 553 total tackles (348 solo), 22 tackles for loss, 7 sacks, 3 interceptions, 24 pass deflections, 6 forced fumbles, 5 fumble recoveries; 4,970 defensive snaps, 593 special teams snaps Jeremy Chinn layin' the BOOM to prevent the catch 💥 pic.twitter.com/rdtk1Cmd2r — NFL (@NFL) October 5, 2025 Standing 6-foot-3 and 220 pounds, Chinn is one of a handful of safeties in the league who have imposing size. The 28-year-old joined Las Vegas last offseason on a two-year, $16.258 million deal ($12.25 million guaranteed) to bolster the loss of Tre’Von Moehrig (Carolina Panthers). And, in a funny twist, Chinn (the Panthers’ second-round pick (64th overall) in the 2020 NFL Draft) notched the second most total tackles (114) in his initial year wearing Silver & Black as a 15-game starter. Notching 996 snaps (100 percent of the defensive snaps Chinn was available), the Southern Illinois’ product brought physicality and versatility to the Patrick Graham-led defense in 2025. With Graham now the defensive boss for the Pittsburgh Steelers and Leonard now in charge of the Raiders defense, Chinn provided insight on the change during minicamp in June. “Yeah, I’m super excited for this defense,” Chinn said after one of the team’s sessions. “Just the different looks, and I don’t want to get into too much detail, but like the different fronts and stuff that we’ll be able to do and incorporate, it’ll just allow me to play a little bit more free and play downhill to the ball.” “I mean, it’s big when it comes down to the style of play, which is really what football is about at the end of the day,” Chinn added when asked about being able to play fast without working about mistakes. “It allows us, like you said, to play fast, play physical, and not have to think too much.” Leonard’s is slated to deploy a fluid scheme that blends elements of coaches he’s learned from — this includes Seattle Seahawks head coach and defensive play caller Mike Macdonald, Minnesota Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores, Kansas City Chiefs defensive boss Steve Spagnuolo, and Graham — to create a player-friendly structure. Leonard deploying Chinn as a hybrid defender who boasts defensive back speed with linebacker size and hitting ability instead of a traditional deep safety is how he gets the most out of talented Indiana native. In his seven seasons in the league, Chinn is at his best when operating closer to the line of scrimmage as his size, speed, and instincts are maximized as a run defender and tackler while mitigating his less-than-ideal coverage skills. This allows the safety to get hands-on with bigger tight ends from the jump and also gives the Raiders a big nickel look where Chinn drops down in the slot. #Raiders S Jeremy Chinn on Arizona safeties Treydan Stukes and Dalton Johnson, both drafted by Las Vegas: "It keeps the offense guessing when we have guys who can play in different spots and rotate different ways… It's been impressive to see those guys be willing to be like,… pic.twitter.com/EBMkw6TqzF — Nick Walters (@nickwalt) June 3, 2026 Simulated pressures and disguised blitz packages are Macdonald’s, Flores’, and Spagnuolo’s calling cards and Leonard dialing those up in Las Vegas will be intriguing to watch. Chinn showcases prime ability to blitz and provides an extra rusher and run stopper with his size. Dropping Chinn into the box or even feigning with the safety moving back in coverage helps Leonard keep offenses honest and on its toes. And can help generate takeaways — an item the Raiders haven’t created more of. The closing speed, ability to diagnose, and explosiveness Chinn brings to the mix is best suited this way to ensure a “see ball, get ball” style of aggressiveness. Arriving with ill intent downhill extenuates his strengths while mitigating exposure as a deep-end cover man. Chinn plays much better with clear intent than backpedaling or chasing in coverage. Which brings us to a key element of Chinn’s game that must be improved: Tackling. From the defensive line, to linebackers, and the secondary, nary a Raiders unit tackled well the last two seasons . From communication and fundamentals breaking down, to taking poor angles, and going for booming hits instead of proper wrap-up and takedown techniques, Las Vegas had the fifth most whiffs amongst the 32 teams in 2025. In terms of percentage of tackles missed, the Raiders notched the fifth-worst mark at 9.8 percent whiffed while the Cincinnati Bengals (who Pro Football Reference charted with a whopping league-leading 170 missed tackles) whiffed on 13 percent. Chinn had the fourth-most missed tackles on the Raiders with 10. Chinn certainly amassed volume but improving the entire defense’s tackling form and efficiency ensures Leonard can have his group playing with its hair on fire. The additions of linebacker Quay Walker and slot cornerback Taron Johnson should provide on-field, lead-by-example types in proper tackling technique, and that becoming infectious to the entire group alongside coaching from Leonard and his defensive assistance should chart a better course. Adding versatile defensive back Treydan Stukes bolsters the Raiders backend coverage ability. Add into that Kubiak’s mantra of players being able to play at multiple positions, the days of seeing Chinn isolated in coverage should become less and less with more talent infused on Las Vegas roster.

title: Las Vegas Raiders mailbag: Will Klint Kubiak, Rob Leonard reel in Maxx Crosby?
summary: Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp is underway with the team wrapping up its first week of practice. Football is finally back as the preseason starts on Thursday with the Hall of Fame game, and the regular season is around the corner. With plenty of excitement in the air, let’s get to this week’s mailbag! Q: […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JULY 29: Maxx Crosby #98 of the Las Vegas Raiders high fives teammates during the first practice of the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images Las Vegas Raiders’ training camp is underway with the team wrapping up its first week of practice. Football is finally back as the preseason starts on Thursday with the Hall of Fame game, and the regular season is around the corner. With plenty of excitement in the air, let’s get to this week’s mailbag! Q: Do you think Klint Kubiak and Rob Leonard will tell Maxx Crosby that he can’t play every snap this year? A: It sounds like Kubiak and Leonard are laying the foundation for this, as one of the first pieces of news from training camp was that they told Crosby to dial it back a bit (h/t ESPN’s Ryan McFadden ). Granted, the primary focus of that conversation seemed to be centered around not hitting the quarterback, essentially saying: “Don’t injure the future of the franchise, Maxx!” But I get the feeling that the overall message to the defensive end is that they want him to be smarter about how he approaches practices and his workload. Now, whether or not Crosby takes that message to heart is a different story. He’s always been a high-motor guy who wants to play every snap, and that’s part of what makes him great. However, at the same time, that’s part of why he’s finished the last two seasons on injured reserve, and being more efficient with his reps/snaps will help improve his longevity. I’m hopeful that Crosby will recognize that he needs to heed the coaching staff’s advice given how the last two years ended, and I’m encouraged that those conversations already seem to be taking place. But, of course, it remains to be seen if he’s actually listening. R8RN8tionEthos Hi Matt, There’s been a lot of dialogue this off season regarding surprise cuts and or surprise starters. One name I don’t believe that has been mentioned is Stokes. With the new reports coming out about Masses being a Spring stand out and earning 1st team reps, how shocked would you be if Stokes ends up being traded, cut, or loses his starting role considering the expectations of McCoy’s talent and Porter coming into his second year, with the potential emergence of 5th round rookie Masses? Can you see this scenario being a possibility? What are your thoughts on it and how would you feel? I think we’d all agree it’s a good thing just as long as they’re playing the best two options. However what’s the reality for such a surprising outcome like this happening? Especially because I believe the consensus has always been Stokes is safe and the only competition is on the other side of the field. A: I’d be pretty shocked if Eric Stokes isn’t a starter to begin the season, barring an injury, of course. He played well enough last year to earn the job, and it seems like the coaching staff has him firmly on the first-team defense because the rotation has exclusively been at the other cornerback spot. Plus, there’s still future value in Stokes since he just turned 27 years old and signed a three-year contract extension in the offseason. Now, in a scenario where Darien Porter, Hezekiah Masses and Jermod McCoy are all playing well, Stokes’ contract is very tradable for the Raiders. The deal includes $20 million fully guaranteed, but only $6 million in signing bonus, so the trade partner would be taking on the bulk of the money and the Raiders wouldn’t have much dead cap hit ($1.2 million per year), according to Over The Cap . That being said, I’d see that happening closer to the trade deadline or in the offseason rather than at the end of training camp in that scenario. From a front office perspective, you want to make sure a young player isn’t just having a good month of practice during training camp and can maintain a high level of play throughout the grind of a 17-game season before making any drastic decisions. Long story short, I think Stokes is pretty much locked in as a starting corner heading into the 2026 season. But nothing is guaranteed beyond that, and the veteran should be looking over his shoulder if the young corners are showing out. 208SilvaRaider With all of the Vita Vea to the Raiders smoke out there, do you think the Raiders will pull off a trade for him? Do you think the Raiders should pull off a trade for him? Seems like he would be a perfect fit on this defense at the weakest position group and the type of player in the middle that makes everyone better. A: I’m conflicted about Vita Vea. On one hand, I love Vea’s game and think he’s one of the best defensive tackles in the NFL. He’d immediately be the second-best defensive player on the Raiders’ roster, and the gap between Vea and Crosby would be pretty narrow. That’s how much I think of the player. However, we’ve talked ad nauseam about how this is a rebuilding year for the Silver and Black where the primary focus is on the future and developing young players. Giving up a draft pick—in what many expect to be a very good class—for a 31-year-old doesn’t align with that strategy. Plus, they’d have to pay him immediately since the reason Vea wants out of Tampa Bay is that he and the Bucs can’t agree on a contract extension. Ultimately, I’d love to see Vea in Las Vegas, but I think the smart move is to hold off on trading for him. Maybe he ends up hitting the free agent market in the offseason, and the Raiders can go after him then without having to give up a coveted draft pick. With how John Spytek operated this spring, I don’t see Spytek making a big swing for Vea. Q: Is there any path for Jackson Powers-Johnson to get back into the starting lineup at one of the two guard spots where he belongs? A: Absolutely. The early reports are that Powers-Johnson and Spencer Burford are the starting guards to begin camp. I’d consider JPJ the favorite to win one of the two jobs, and he clearly has an early lead over Caleb Rogers, Jordan Meredith and Trey Zuhn III. With a good summer, the 2024 second-round pick should be a first-stringer on Sept. 13. Q: Who will start at free safety against the Dolphins? And who will be the next man up there? A: This is a pair of million-dollar questions that I wish I had better answers to, LOL! I dove into more detail on this last week ( hyperlink ); to me, Treydan Stukes is the favorite to start at free safety. The problem is Stukes doesn’t have much experience playing the position right now, but he was versatile at Arizona and has the traits to make a smooth transition in the NFL. After that, option B is probably just running it back with Isaiah Pola-Mao. However, that didn’t work out well last year, so maybe Dalton Johnson gets a shot as the next man up. Johnson was also a versatile defensive back at Arizona, and he took a decent amount of snaps on the backend of the defense in college. I think he’s more of a strong safety/big nickel in the NFL, but this is kind of an experimental season for the Raiders, so I wouldn’t be opposed to giving him a shot at free safety. The options are pretty limited without a clear choice at the position; might as well see what the fifth-rounder can do. Q: What role will Trey Zuhn have this coming season? Is he strictly a guard? A: According to ESPN’s Ryan McFadden , Zuhn has already been getting snaps at center with the second-team offense, switching back and forth with Meredith. I also wouldn’t be surprised if the rookie gets some run at right tackle, especially if both DJ Glaze and Charles Grant are struggling early on in training camp. Zuhn’s versatility is one of his biggest calling cards, giving him a chance to earn a starting spot at one of the three open competitions in the trenches. That being said, he’s most likely destined to be a versatile backup in year one, a “sixth-man” of the o-line, if you will. Q: I’m bummed about Laki Tasi getting waived. What was the…

summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are switching to a 3-4 defense in 2026, which puts them in need of a nose tackle. title: Raiders News: Klint Kubiak provides early update on Fernando Mendoza, quarterback competition in training camp
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders are only about a week into practice, but the biggest storyline from Raiders’ training camp is monitoring the quarterback situation and, more specifically, rookie Fernando Mendoza. That comes with the territory of taking a signal-caller with the first overall pick of the draft, as the fanbase wants to know how the […]
full_text: HENDERSON, NEVADA - JULY 29: Fernando Mendoza #15 of the Las Vegas Raiders looks to pass during the first practice of the team's training camp at the Las Vegas Raiders Headquarters/Intermountain Health Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Henderson, Nevada. (Photo by Ian Maule/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders are only about a week into practice, but the biggest storyline from Raiders’ training camp is monitoring the quarterback situation and, more specifically, rookie Fernando Mendoza. That comes with the territory of taking a signal-caller with the first overall pick of the draft, as the fanbase wants to know how the future of the franchise is looking. So head coach Klint Kubiak should expect to get questions about Mendoza and the most important position on the field throughout camp, and the topic was brought up after Friday’s practice. Kubiak said that he’s “pleased” with where all the quarterbacks are right now and their work ethic, noting that the position battle has had a “positive start”. He also mentioned that Mendoza, along with expected third-stringer Aidan O’Connell, have been pushing Kirk Cousins, who was officially named the starter to begin training camp. “Anytime [Mendoza or O’Connell] complete a ball better than [Cousins] does or get it out faster than he does, then he should get pissed and want to do it better; that’s the goal,” the coach said. “And I think they’ve done that in these first three practices. Every guy is doing something good every day, and it makes the other guy want to stay after practice a little bit longer to work on that throw that they missed. So, it’s a really bright room. Coach Sullivan is doing a great job.” As for Mendoza, specifically, Kubiak shed some light on how the rookie can grow and how he’s handling criticism. “I love the mindset that he has,” Kubiak replied. “That’s what all of our players should have. Nobody has arrived, especially a rookie quarterback. So, you just keep giving them a new rep every day, and coach from it, and go back the next day, solve the problem, and go to work and fix a new problem. He’s just like everybody else that’s got to earn their way. “…He’s very coachable, all the quarterbacks are. Really, all of our players are. We’ve got guys that want to get better. So, when they’re eager to get better, you better make sure you’re on it as a coach. So, we’ve got to challenge ourselves as coaches and make sure that we’re giving them the right coaching points and helping them get to where they want to get to.” In summary, it’s all positive from the early stages of camp. However, the first true stress tests won’t come until the team puts the pads on next week, and then when the Arizona Cardinals roll into Las Vegas for the first preseason game on Aug. 13. In Other Raiders’ Links: Kwity Paye OK: After a scare in practice where Paye went down and did not return, Kubiak said the edge defender avoided a serious injury , and the team is just trying to play it safe at this stage. Mendoza Mania National Championship: The culmination of the summer series, diving into the Heisman Trophy winner’s performance on the big stage . Raiders listed as fit for Vita Vea: “Second-year general manager John Spytek was a longtime Buccaneers executive who played a role in drafting Vea out of Washington in 2018,” ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler wrote. “The Raiders’ current defensive tackles are a journeyman (Adam Butler) and a promising 2024 seventh-rounder (Jonah Laulu). So there’s plenty of room for reinforcements.” Mendoza fine with QB2 role: “‘Whatever decisions are made at the end, that’s fantastic — and I’m well for it,’” the first overall draft pick said, via ESPN’s Ryan McFadden . “‘I just want the team to win, so that’s where I’m at.’”

summary: This past week, I asked the following question: Whether you’re watching from home or cheering from the stands, what are your favorite game-day rituals and traditions? Do you have specific tailgating rituals if you attend the game in person? Do you have other rituals, lucky team swag you wear, or specific foods or drinks you […]
full_text: Sept. 25, 2016 Tailgating at the game between the Cleveland Browns and the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami Gardens, Fla. (Photo by Michele Eve Sandberg/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images This past week, I asked the following question: Whether you’re watching from home or cheering from the stands, what are your favorite game-day rituals and traditions? Do you have specific tailgating rituals if you attend the game in person? Do you have other rituals, lucky team swag you wear, or specific foods or drinks you have? Below are some of your thoughts and answers UpInPensacola has some delicious-sounding foods on deck for gameday. Turn on the TVs in the kitchen and Florida room. Have Sunday lunch getting in the pipeline by 10:30 and done at 12:45 PM, which is normally around the end of the first quarter. Often gumbos/shrimp creole (Saints) and palomilla steak or black beans/rice/chicken (Dolphins). Water and tea in the hot months. Beer and wine in the cooler ones. There WILL be screaming and whooping! Neighbors beware. (Dog often runs away to another room with touchdowns, while neighbor’s dogs bark back.) VolFaninFla does some praying pre-game, which seems appropriate given what we have seen from this team in the past. Since games are normally on Sunday, heavy prayer they don’t lose but usually to no avail. Bill Moody has a routine that might get changed up this coming season. 1. Check Fantasy News for any last minute line-up adjustments (for injuries only, otherwise, I don’t do last minute switcher as I spent all week picking the best guy) 2. Head to Pizza Place and watch games with friends (when Miami has a 10am Pacific start time). 3. Watch the late game at home. I’ll probably switch it up this year: 1. Check Fantasty News 2. BBQ and play Magic the Gathering with friends all day, put redzone on in the background. 3. Watch the late game if its interesting, otherwise, play Fortnite or watch a show. 4. Catch highlights before bed. TheRoo1 saves his drink until the Phins score a touchdown. Wondering what he felt like after the Phins blew out the Broncos a couple of seasons back. I put a few premium ales on ice, and dont open one until the Phins score a td. Have a feeling I wont be drinking much this year. Phoenix6 fondly remembers when those kids were still living at home. We all miss that once our kids grow up! Those are wonderful items of tradition James. I used to have great fun with my boys as they grew up. We’d hoop & holler as we watched, to the dismay of their mother LMAO. Now up in age plus other circumstances as I aged, I haven’t done anything. I still root like hell though! And my sons and I talk a lot about our team & games. Dolphster likes that I fly the Canes flag in Gator country and once had some food rituals that have since fallen by the wayside. James, I love the fact that you fly your Hurricanes flag in Gainesville! I don’t really have any pregame rituals anymore, but in my 20s when I lived in Broward County, before watching every game on TV, I would go to Tarks in Dania Beach and pick up wings and steamed shrimp to take home and have while watching the game. Well, that’s a solid list of things that us fans do or used to do, but sadly it’s the somewhat dead part of the year for the site, so there were not a lot of responses on this one. If you missed the original post, please share your game day rituals in the comments section below. As always, thank you to each of you who take the time to read these posts and answer our question of the day.

title: Sunday Patriots Notes: Eli Raridon impressing early in training camp
summary: The New England Patriots’ training camp is fully underway. Following three straight padded practices to conclude the first week, the team is off on Sunday before getting back to work. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week that was. Welcome to the latest installment of […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA- JUNE 11: Eli Raridon #82 of the New England Patriots speaks to the media after New England Patriots Minicamp on June 11, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Summer Lamont/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots’ training camp is fully underway. Following three straight padded practices to conclude the first week, the team is off on Sunday before getting back to work. Before we focus on what lies ahead, however, let’s take one final look back at the week that was. Welcome to the latest installment of our Sunday Patriots Notes . Raridon’s hot start Through seven training camp practices, it’s been hard to miss rookie tight end Eli Raridon. Raridon has been active as a pass catcher this summer, often threatening New England’s up the seam and running away from second-level defenders across the field. On Friday, that led to the rookie catching multiple passes during 7-on-7s, including a touchdown in the corner of the end zone from Drake Maye — a unit he is regularly been apart of as the team’s No. 2 tight end. “He is a big dude, first off, that can run. I mean, that’s pretty cool, and he is smart,” Maye said. “He went to Notre Dame and I know he is another guy that, half ACC, half not, but we like to call ourselves smart in the ACC so— He understands positions, he understands how to play both positions, the tight end spot. I think he is making plays on the football. That’s what you want to see from a young guy, and he is putting the work in. “That is the biggest thing with a young rookie. You want to see him go out there and take a rep when he is tired and not call for a sub, and he is doing all the things the right way, and I am looking forward to seeing what he does throughout camp. He has been a great player for us and a great dude.” While Raridon has seen his fair share of reps with Maye and the first-team offense, the rookie remains slotted behind veteran Hunter Henry on the depth chart. That has also led to plenty of work with backup quarterback Tommy DeVito, who has no issues peppering the tight end with targets. “Have you seen him? That’s a big target. I bet you’d want to throw to him too,” DeVito said. “I mean, he’s big, he’s athletic, his confidence is growing. Trying to get more savvy with the offense, like as it’s going. But that just comes with time and how many reps he gets. So, just keep trying to get as many reps as we can. I know he’s got a lot of information coming at him. I know I’ve been a rookie before in a situation like this. So just keep him encouraged, keep him going. But he’s got awesome hands, he’s got the frame. He’s got everything going for him. So, I’m looking forward to seeing how he plays this year.” A quiet spring from Raridon, coupled with a season-ending injury to veteran free-agent addition Julian Hill, left the door open for a potential free agent addition at the position. While there is still work to be done for the 2026 third-round pick, Raridon’s emergence early in camp has him trending toward earning a role as a rookie. “You can see the game slowing down for him a little bit,” Hunter Henry said. “Every single time he gets reps, he learns from those reps. He’s watching them in the film room. We’re talking about things. He’s got a bright future ahead of him for sure.” CB depth The Patriots depth at cornerback has been tested early in camp with Carlton Davis (unknown) sidelined for the last three practices after leaving Tuesday’s session early. Charles Woods has consistently been first up in his place. “Just having a full offseason in the system now, I’m more comfortable with the play calling. I’m understanding the scheme, what we’re trying to get done as a defense, and now just going out there and playing football,” said Woods, who spent last season as the No. 4 cornerback after being claimed off waivers during cutdown day. With Christian Gonzalez (rest) then limited on Saturday, Kobee Minor, Kindle Vildor, and fifth-round pick Karon Prunty saw elevated snaps. Prunty made the most of it with an interception off of DeVito while Minor also recorded a pass breakup. That group will continue to sort itself out over the next few weeks with roster spots limited. Gonzo update Beyond being a limited participant on Saturday due to rest reasons, Christian Gonzalez has remained a full participant in padded practices as he searches for a contract extension. Mike Vrabel has appreciated that approach from his top cornerback this offseason, but did not have an update on where negotiations stood. “It’ll either get done, and when it gets done, that’ll be the progress that’s made,” Vrabel said Saturday. “Everybody that’s involved is working hard. I cannot express the professionalism that Gonzo has started camp with. It’s clear that he wants to improve, that he wants to be the best at his craft and at that position. I think that he’s made that known by the way he’s come out here to practice.” Underrated names Training camp always provides a chance for underrated players to make a push for roster spots. Through seven practices, here are some who have caught our eyes: RB Jam Miller: While New England’s defensive front has largely won the rushing periods, Miller has caught the eye on numerous occasions for his quickness and ability to find holes. Lan Larison still seems like the top RB3, but Miller could make a push. WR Cameron Dorner: Dorner has been stacking positive days together which was recently rewarded with a handful of reps with Tommy DeVito and the second string offense. The UDFA receiver has shown the ability to separate and while the wide receiver depth chart is crowded, New England lost practice squader Jeremiah Webb for the season. Dorner is making an early case to stick around in that capacity. TE Tanner Arkin: Perhaps no longer underrated as the UDFA has consistently seen time with the top offense due to his blocking ability. That ability has slotted him in nicely behind Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon, and Arkin’s blocking ability has created some short play-action opportunities through the air. LB Khalil Jacobs: On the defensive side of the ball, Jacobs has repped next to K.J. Britt and Chad Muma recently on the second team defense. He logged a pressure in Saturday’s practice and has been around the ball often in run defense from the off-ball linebacker spot. Chism’s growth Efton Chism and Mack Hollins quickly developed a strong relationship during Chism’s rookie season as they would often be two of the first people in the facility. The two enjoy pushing each other to get better and Chism calls Hollins one of his best friends, but the veteran has enjoyed seeing the 24-year old’s growth in Year 2. “I think the biggest thing is now he’s taken anything that he was with me doing last year, and he’s molded it. And like I told him, take everything I do, and then change to what’s best for you. And that’s what I’ve seen him do,” Hollins said. “It’s been it’s been really cool to watch him grow not only as a player on the field, but off in understanding how to be a pro and things it takes to be great and sustain that for more than a season and not just be like, ‘Oh, it’s a guy that is shining in a training camp for one year cause he’s small and white.’ Efton’s a baller, that’s why he’s shining.” WR room Chism will have work to do to make the 53-man roster again this season after the team added A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs to pair with him and Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, DeMario Douglas, and Kayshon Boutte. Keeping all seven wide receivers on the Week 1 roster feels like a stretch, which means one will be the odd man out. That could be still be Kayshon Boutte, who remains open to a trade after requesting one back in the spring, which would open the door for youngsters like Chism and Kyle Williams, who would remain a surprise cut, to remain off waivers. “I love having depth, but I would say that we’re always going to try to look to…

title: Tanner Arkin ‘learning quickly’ amid first-team reps, says Mike Vrabel
summary: After the New England Patriots secured a Super Bowl appearance just six months ago and put together an offseason highlighted by key additions, it’s difficult to find vulnerabilities on a roster poised for improvement in 2026. However, with multi-year free-agent signing Julian Hill placed on season-ending injured reserve in the spring due to a knee […]
full_text: Jul 25, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots tight end Tanner Arkin (84) looks on after a drill at training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect After the New England Patriots secured a Super Bowl appearance just six months ago and put together an offseason highlighted by key additions, it’s difficult to find vulnerabilities on a roster poised for improvement in 2026. However, with multi-year free-agent signing Julian Hill placed on season-ending injured reserve in the spring due to a knee injury, the Patriots need a blocking tight end for their final roster in August. Just seven practices into training camp, undrafted tight end Tanner Arkin looks equipped for that role as the number of his first-team reps increases. “Just the learning each and every day,” head coach Mike Vrabel said before Saturday’s practice when asked what about Arkin has impressed him. “The competitive spirit, going against [Dre’Mont Jones] and Elijah [Ponder], trying to block, be consistent and be physical. “He’s learned what to do quickly. I think sometimes, young players, when things start to pile on, they can slow down because they’re thinking a little bit. I haven’t seen that, so hopefully that continues.” The Illinois product is currently mixing snaps between the first- and second-team offenses. With Drake Maye’s unit, he lines up as an in-line blocker, where he’s also been found as a receiving option during the last two practices. On Saturday, Maye connected with Arkin wide open in the flat, as the rookie leaked out of the formation off a play-action delayed route and added some yards after the catch. “I think for me, it’s taking it bit by bit, piece by piece,” the 23-year-old said after practice about how he studies the playbook. “I think [the coaches] do a good job with each install, kind of breaking it down … Coach Brown, my tight end coach, coaches in such a great amount of detail that allows me to learn at a quick pace.” Following his final season with the Fighting Illini in 2025, Arkin declared for the NFL draft, entering the pre-draft process known for his physicality as a run blocker — a trait he said he takes pride in. Arkin achieved a 79.5 run-blocking grade on Pro Football Focus that year. Still, without hearing his name called on draft night, Arkin’s journey to the league wasn’t a traditional one. The Fort Collins, Colo., native had interest from a couple of franchises, but he, his family and agent collectively agreed that New England was the best option. Arkin added that he’s thankful for the chance to land with such an “awesome team” that possesses a “great” team culture. “It’s been going great,” Arkin said about his experience during the summer sessions. “You know, it’s kind of surreal to be here at the pro level, and just to be able to get this opportunity is amazing. So, I’m just taking it day by day and really soaking it in, trying to get better.” As the tight end works to improve and secure a spot on the final roster, 31-year-old Hunter Henry, entering his 11th season, has been a resource for Arkin as he acclimates to an NFL environment in Foxboro. “Hunter’s awesome,” Arkin said. “I’ve been watching him for years. He’s such a great tight end, and he’s been around the league. He’s a man of great character. And just to have a guy like that in the room has been great to have a few conversations and just watch what he does on a day-to-day basis and learn from that.” Henry also praised Arkin for his effort and development, noting the UDFA has been performing well. “Tanner’s doing a lot of good things,” Henry said Saturday on what he’s seen from Arkin this offseason. “Every day, [he’s] plugging away, doing a lot of mixing in there with us on the [first team] and the [second team]. Wherever he can earn a role, he’s just trying to do as much as he can, and he’s doing a lot of good things.”
