title: 7 performances of note from the Patriots’ seventh training camp practice
summary: For a third straight day, the New England Patriots put on their full pads on Saturday. Intensity was not as high as the last two days as several veterans were managed, but plenty of work still was done. To recap the seventh practice of the summer, please make sure to head over to our Patriots […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Kyle Williams (18) runs after making a catch during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect For a third straight day, the New England Patriots put on their full pads on Saturday. Intensity was not as high as the last two days as several veterans were managed, but plenty of work still was done. To recap the seventh practice of the summer, please make sure to head over to our Patriots training camp notebook . In the meantime, here is who caught our eye during the session. Standout of the day WR Romeo Doubs: The $68 million man has seen a slow start to his Patriots’ tenure on the practice fields. That flipped on Saturday as Doubs led all of Drake Maye’s pass catchers with five targets and managed to haul in all of them during 7-on-7s and full-team work. The duo struck multiple times over the middle of the field a day after Doubs made an impressive grab in the end zone for a touchdown. Doubs’ did appear to put the football on the ground at one point at the end of a play, but it was on overall positive practice for the 26-year old. Other performances of note WR A.J. Brown: Doubs was not the only offseason addition to continue stacking strong days on Saturday, as A.J. Brown continued to look more in-sync with Drake Maye. Brown caught all three of his targets from Maye with his best work coming as he muscled a contested target away from Christian Gonzalez. The 29-year old receiver also added quick hitters on an out and slant before leaving practice early for what appeared to be rest related. DBs Karon Prunty and Dell Pettus: New England’s secondary got their hands on multiple footballs on Saturday, which began with safety Dell Pettus jumping in front of a pass from Drake Maye to Mack Hollins to record an interception. Shortly after, rookie cornerback Karon Prunty hauled in an interception of his own as he impressively tracked a deep ball from Tommy DeVito to Cameron Dorner. WRs Kyle Williams and Efton Chism III: As the Patriots’ top two pass catchers continued to build positive momentum, two of their younger depth options did as well. While Kyle Williams got open downfield but could not connect on a deep bomb from Maye, the speedster totaled three catches from Tommy DeVito as he impressively worked through contact to snag a hole shot and comeback route along the sideline. Behind him, Efton Chism III got open over the middle of the field on numerous occasions which resulted in two receptions from DeVito, while Chism also saw a pair of manufactured touches (one from Drake Maye). K Andy Borregales: Appearing to work from a further distance than usual this summer — with the long coming from roughly 55 yards out — Andy Borregales continued to impress this summer. The sophomore kicker looked to connect on all five of his field goal attempts on Saturday as he is now 21-of-23 for the summer. The Patriots will be off on Sunday before holding their eighth training camp practice on Monday. Gates are scheduled to open at 9:15 a.m. ET for that session, with practice again set to start approximately an hour later.

title: Patriots’ rookie Gabe Jacas participates in first practice
summary: Patriots rookie outside linebacker Gabe Jacas made his NFL practice debut Saturday. After starting training camp on the active/non-football injury list, Jacas passed his physical and returned to the practice field. “We’ll get Gabe back today,” Mike Vrabel said Saturday morning. “He’ll be out there in a limited role. We’ve talked to you about the […]
full_text: BLOOMINGTON, IN - SEPTEMBER 20: Gabe Jacas #17 of the Illinois Fighting Illini looks on during a college football game against the Indiana Hoosiers on September 20, 2025 at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Indiana. (Photo by Joe Robbins/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Patriots rookie outside linebacker Gabe Jacas made his NFL practice debut Saturday. After starting training camp on the active/non-football injury list, Jacas passed his physical and returned to the practice field. “We’ll get Gabe back today,” Mike Vrabel said Saturday morning. “He’ll be out there in a limited role. We’ve talked to you about the return to play protocol that we have, and so now he gets handed over to the coaches, and that’ll be in a limited role. He won’t be involved in the team reps, but hopefully Monday, we’ll see him back out there.” The beginning of Jacas’ Patriots career has been turbulent after being drafted in the second round of the NFL Draft this spring. After missing the offseason workout program following a knee procedure, Jacas was one of the last draft picks in the league to sign his rookie contract — a deal that included an uncommon injury waiver. Since signing his contract last Saturday, Jacas has been focused on his return-to-play rehab. Vrabel shared the rookie did not enjoy being sidelined, which quickly became evident during his first practice when he bulldozed outside linebackers coach Mike Smith during an individual drill. Gabe Jacas is off to a hot start pic.twitter.com/wHCwQDlMJF — Matt Dolloff (@RealMattDolloff) August 1, 2026 “He loves football. He’s been itching to get back,” Vrabel said. “He texts me all the time. He texts me late at night, ‘Hey, am I going to practice tomorrow?’ I’m like, ‘No, just like I told you at 6:30 last night or tonight that you’re not going to practice tomorrow. You don’t have to text me at 10:00 and ask again. The answer is still no, not yet.’ “You want that. You want guys that are looking for ways in as opposed to looking for ways out. I think he just wants to get out there, get acclimated and be with his teammates. That is all he wants to do. He just wants to play football.” The Patriots will be off on Sunday before returning to the practice fields on Monday.

title: Patriots training camp recap: Offseason additions active at wide receiver
summary: While the pads remained on for the New England Patriots on Saturday, the practice scripts were thrown away as Mike Vrabel and the coaching staff instead simulated in-game drives. “There is no script, so the players won’t have what the play is or what the situation is, which we always like to do here, and […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Romeo Doubs (87) makes a catch during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect While the pads remained on for the New England Patriots on Saturday, the practice scripts were thrown away as Mike Vrabel and the coaching staff instead simulated in-game drives. “There is no script, so the players won’t have what the play is or what the situation is, which we always like to do here, and give them an opportunity to go play, get into a little bit of rhythm, get into a little bit of conditioning, create a drive,“ Vrabel explained. Even in a simulated session with full pads, it was more of a low-key day at times but plenty of work was done on the practice fields behind Gillette Stadium. Here’s what went down. Attendance Absent: CB Carlton Davis III, OG Alijah Vera-Tucker (new/rest), FB Reggie Gilliam (new) Returnee: DT Christian Barmore Limited: OT Morgan Moses, WR A.J. Brown, CB Christian Gonzalez, CB Marcus Jones, RB Rhamondre Stevenson, ED Gabe Jacas PUP/NFI: RB Terrell Jennings, TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, S Brenden Schooler Injuries: OG Caedan Wallace, OT James Hudson For their third straight padded practice, Mike Vrabel gave several veterans limited workloads as they departed practice early while Morgan Moses just participated in competitive periods. “There is just trying to have a plan for everybody and try to finish this third day off really well,” Vrabel said. “Like we always talk about, whether those guys are out there or not, that provides opportunities for other players, and we’ve seen guys do well with those opportunities that they’ve been given.” New England did remain without Carlton Davis for the third straight practice, while depth offensive lineman Caedan Wallace and James Hudson were banged up at various parts of practice and spent time with the training staff. In a positive development, rookie pass rusher Gabe Jacas was activated off the NFI list and participated in a limited capacity (no full-team work) on Saturday. Takeaways Brown and Doubs: It’s been a relatively quiet start to training camp for free agent addition Romeo Doubs, but the 26-year old had his most productive practice of the day on Saturday. Starting in 7-on-7s, Doubs hauled in a pair of passes from Maye over the middle of the field before going on to catch all three of his targets in full-team work. The lone blemish may have been a fumble on his final reception (although the whistle may have blown the play dead). As for fellow offseason addition A.J. Brown, the top receiver caught all three of his targets from Drake Maye — including a contested ball against Gonzalez — before departing. Additionally at wide receiver, DeMario Douglas had downfield receptions from both Maye and Tommy DeVito. Kyle Williams could not connect on his deep ball from Maye, but had three catches from DeVito with two coming through contact. Fellow second-year receiver Efton Chism then had two receptions from DeVito over the middle and a pair of manufactured touches. Doubs and Williams both appeared to be banged up at times but finished practice. Defensive turnovers: It has been multiple practices since the Patriots secondary has forced a turnover — let alone an incompletion as Drake Maye has been extremely efficient in two padded practices. On Saturday, New England’s defense got on the board as safety Dell Pettus jumped a throw to Mack Hollins for an interception. Pettus, who had numerous competitive plays in the secondary today, was not the only defensive back to haul in an interception as rookie cornerback Karon Prunty used his high school wide receiver background to track and intercept a deep ball from Tommy DeVito. Rookie CB Karon Prunty with one of two interceptions in practice today … credits his high school WR background for helping track the deep throw by Tommy DeVito. pic.twitter.com/J7egBepGN2 — Brian Hines (@iambrianhines) August 1, 2026 Maye’s day: After back-to-back impressive days for Drake Maye, the quarterback’s performance on Saturday was a slight step below highlighted by the interception to Pettus and an overthrow while targeting Kayshon Boutte. But even in a day with a few blemishes, Maye still delivered on several downfield throws which included a contested catch by A.J. Brown working through Christian Gonzalez and completions to Boutte on a pretty back shoulder ball and DeMario Douglas. Accurate Andy: New England’s sophomore kicker Andy Borregales does not have any competition this training camp, and his performance to date has proved why. On Saturday, Borregales appeared to connect on all five of his field goal attempts with the distance moving back from prior practices — as his final kick seemed to come from roughly 55 yards out. Through seven practices, Borregales is now 21-of-23 on his attempts. Other notes: With Rhamondre Stevenson limited, TreVeyon Henderson operated as the top back with Lan Larison behind him. Larison put the ball on the ground once on a screen while running lanes remained limited besides one notable run up the middle from Henderson. UDFA tight end Tanner Arkin continues to rep with the first-team and caught a play-action bootleg in the flat from Maye. With Alijah Vera-Tucker limited, Ben Brown served as the starting left guard. Caleb Lomu repped at right tackle when Morgan Moses was out. Dre’Mont Jones was in the backfield off a stunt for what likely would have been a sack, while Elijah Ponder continued to be notable along the edge as well. Bradyn Swinson and rookie Quintayvious Hutchins had strong showing in 1-on-1s. Joshua Farmer had strong reps along the interior in 1-on-1s and was quickly in the backfield on one instance for a run stuff. At linebacker, Chad Muma was often around the football in the run game coming downhill while Christian Elliss had an impressive pass breakup in 7s downfield on Pop Douglas. Charles Woods remained the top backup cornerback in place of Carlton Davis. With Gonzalez then limited, Kobee Minor, Kindle Vildor, and Prunty got work in his place. The Patriots will be off on Sunday before returning to practice on Monday, which is set to begin at 10:15 a.m. ET.

summary: The New England Patriots will close out their second block of practices on Saturday. For a third straight day, the reigning AFC champions will hit the Gillette Stadium fields before a second off-day on Sunday. Here is all you need to know about training camp practice No. 7. Schedule The seventh practice of this year’s […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - MAY 27: Lan Larison #34 of the New England Patriots carries during New England Patriots OTA on May 27, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New England Patriots will close out their second block of practices on Saturday. For a third straight day, the reigning AFC champions will hit the Gillette Stadium fields before a second off-day on Sunday. Here is all you need to know about training camp practice No. 7. Schedule The seventh practice of this year’s training camp will again take place on the fields behind Gillette Stadium. As usual, parking and attendance are free. 9:30 a.m. ET: Mike Vrabel press conference 10:15 a.m. ET: Practice ca. 12:15 p.m. ET: Player availability (QB Behren Morton, TE Hunter Henry, TE Tanner Arkin, LB Robert Spillane, CB Marcus Jones, CB Karon Prunty) As always, of course, the schedule is tentative and subject to change. For more information, please visit our Pats Pulpit Training Camp Guide . Story of the day How intense will the session be? After back-to-back days of practicing in full pads, will Mike Vrabel give his team a breather on Saturday? Or, with the second off-day of camp coming up, will he opt for more intensity and full-speed competition? Arguments can be made for both, buy with only so many practice opportunities during the summer staying in full pads would not come as a surprise. Injuries to monitor NFI: RB Terrell Jennings, S Brenden Schooler PUP: TE C.J. Dippre, ED Harold Landry III, ED Gabe Jacas Injured: CB Carlton Davis III TBD: DT Christian Barmore Christian Barmore was a surprise no-show on Friday, joining the injured Carlton Davis as well as the five players on the physically unable to perform and non-football injury lists on the sidelines. Whether his absence is injury-related is not known at the moment, but he did not appear to get banged up during Thursday’s practice. Players to watch WR Kayshon Boutte: The most notable of the Patriots’ pass catchers during the ramp-up period, Boutte has been quiet the last two days. Maybe that is a result of the practice script, or maybe of the tide turning in the receiver room. Regardless, others have taken center stage since the introduction of full pads on Thursday. LG Alijah-Vera Tucker and OT Morgan Moses: The two veterans were in and out of the lineup on Friday, which might have contributed to the defense finding some success out of its pressure packages. The hope will be that a potential return to increased participation on Saturday will help shore things up again up front. The returners: The Patriots practiced competitive kickoff returns for the first time on Friday, which would suggest that Saturday might see some punt drills on the menu. If so, will Kyle Williams, Lan Larison and Eftom Chism remain active? Pats Pulpit will have you covered throughout the day, so please make sure to regularly check back to patspulpit.com for all the latest news from camp. Credentialed Patriots beat writers Brian Hines ( @iambrianhines ), Andrew Guindon ( @NestPgs ) Taylor Kyles ( @tkyles39 ) will bring you live updates from camp on their Twitter/X feeds, so please make sure to give them a follow.

title: 3-Point Stance: Patriots’ training camp expectations have changed
summary: The 2024 season left the New England Patriots in a bleak spot. New England finished the season with a 4-13 record and moved on from Jerod Mayo as head coach after just one season. The only factors offering the fan base hope were 2024 third overall pick Drake Maye making a potential leap and new […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - July 25: New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel at training camp on July 25, 2026. (Photo by John Tlumacki/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images The 2024 season left the New England Patriots in a bleak spot. New England finished the season with a 4-13 record and moved on from Jerod Mayo as head coach after just one season. The only factors offering the fan base hope were 2024 third overall pick Drake Maye making a potential leap and new head coach Mike Vrabel building a competitive culture and foundation in year one. But none of that was guaranteed. Still, everything seemed to go right for the Patriots. They made the Super Bowl last season as champions of the AFC, which was a surprise to a majority of NFL fans and media, who had lower expectations. Maye also became an MVP finalist while Vrabel put together one of the most well-rounded coaching staffs in the league, raising the floor of the team and elevating the franchise’s player development pipeline. As a result, expectations entering training camp have changed from a year ago. Eyeing cohesiveness over individual player development In 2025, Vrabel’s goals for his players heading into the summer sessions were built on creating a foundation: building a team, earning a role and preparing to win. “We have to start coming together as a football team,” Vrabel said ahead of last summer’s first practice. “The other thing is [the players] have to earn a role, and that’s a great time for them to personally earn a role through training camp, what they can do for the team, how they can help us and how they can help themselves.” Leading into 2026, however, that approach has changed in Vrabel’s second season with New England, wanting to expand on the team’s season success as starters established themselves. “The expectations always get higher … Our job is to recreate the things that we did really well last year, the culture, the ability to win different ways, to find ways to win, understand how to win and how to prepare,” Vrabel said before practice on July 25. “We’re going to have a more difficult journey.” From an evaluation standpoint, the emphasis last year was centered on tracking the progression of young talent and identifying potential long-term starters. Maye was the focal point, with each practice offering another opportunity to evaluate his development and ability to lead the first-team offense. But through a championship-level lens, the attention has now shifted to how well each unit orchestrates as a collective group; it’s about how Maye is meshing with the new offensive pieces as they get acclimated to a new scheme. One of the biggest storylines of camp, for instance, is his connection with A.J. Brown, which progressed from an out-of-rhythm start to four completions on Thursday and a 50-yard touchdown the following practice. We’re nitpicking the details that could determine whether they can raise banner No. 7, like the tight end room’s needed young talent and Cory Durden’s transition to becoming the starting nose tackle. Schematic expansion and fine-tuning schemes En route to building one cohesive group at each unit, part of the change this summer is conducted within the playbooks. In the spring, quarterbacks coach Ashton Grant mentioned the coaching staff trying to “weaponize” the quarterbacks’ minds. And of course, as the starter, much of that responsibility to improve mental processing falls on Maye. Rather than proving he can lead the offense, training camp is now about determining how much more responsibility Maye can handle making adjustments at the line of scrimmage as offensive coordinator Josh McDaniels expands on his scheme. The same principle applies to Zak Kuhr’s defense as well. Back in February, Vrabel called for his staff at all three units to bring him “fresh ideas” for 2026. Both staffs identified over the offseason what worked last year and what didn’t, correspondingly adding pieces throughout the calendar break to fine-tune areas of the roster they felt needed change. Left guard Alijah Vera-Tucker was signed to bolster the point of attack for both Maye and the ground game. Meanwhile, second-round pick Gabe Jacas and free-agency signing Dre’Mont Jones were brought in on the defensive edge to help turn pressures into sacks — the primary shortcoming of a largely successful defense in 2025. Veterans sustaining the team culture The team culture Vrabel guided his players into cementing last year was a driving variable for why outside talent came to Foxboro in free agency. “I think it comes down to Vrabel coming in and establishing that culture where everybody has real love for each other, wants to play for each other, and wants to do everything they can on that field,” Vera-Tucker said earlier this offseason. “All those factors came into play in the decision to come here.” Vrabel overhauled the Patriots’ roster entering 2025, resetting around 50% of the roster he originally inherited from the season prior. Currently, a large majority of 2025’s active roster is intact as the franchise selectively upgraded. Instead of Vrabel building the culture from scratch, returning players and New England’s veterans are now tasked with establishing that camaraderie with those new additions.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Efton Chism leaning on mental growth entering second season
summary: Getting ready to enter the NFL as a rookie, the focus for Efton Chism III was preparing for the physicality of the league. After signing with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent, Chism went on to make the 53-man roster following a standout training camp and preseason. Entering Year 2, his offseason focus then […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Efton Chism III (86) makes a catch during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Getting ready to enter the NFL as a rookie, the focus for Efton Chism III was preparing for the physicality of the league. After signing with the Patriots as an undrafted free agent, Chism went on to make the 53-man roster following a standout training camp and preseason. Entering Year 2, his offseason focus then shifted to the mental side of the game. “How can I stay on top of my playbook, stay watching film, keep doing all those little things to where when I get back I can still talk coverages, I can still talk plays and not feel like I’m three months behind or trying to catch up to the veterans how I felt when I first got here. So that I think was probably the biggest thing I did this offseason,” Chism said. “Obviously speed training, always trying to get bigger, faster, stronger. But I think mentally that was a huge thing for me this offseason.” His wide receiver coach quickly noticed the progression. “Understanding the details a little bit better,” Todd Downing said during minicamp. “I think he had some exposure last year when Mack [Hollins] went out of moving around in different spots. That’s accelerating and improving as well this offseason. Being able to walk in and know what a concept is or what the formation is without having to think about it is going to help him play faster when the ball is snapped.” After making the 53-man roster as a rookie, Chism appeared in eight regular season games, catching three passes for 75 yards and a touchdown. He then added a 20-yard reception in the Patriots’ Wild Card victory over the Los Angeles Chargers. The additions of A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs have only made the Patriots’ wide receiver room more competitive entering 2026, but Chism has embraced that reality and has continued to make plays this summer. Efton Chism athletic touchdown catch pic.twitter.com/2ajoQUSmKn — Savage (@Savageboston) July 31, 2026 “I think as I’m starting to understand the NFL, I think every year is going to be like that,” Chism said. “That’s kind of a mindset I feel like I’ve adjusted to. It’s like every year, all of us are competing. We all want to play. We all want to make plays, and that’s just the nature of the NFL. “So, I’m excited for it, and I appreciate it and I think competition makes us all better. I think me and Pop competing makes us better. I think Kayshon and A.J. make each other better. Everyone in the whole room, like we’re all trying to make each other better each and every day.”
author: Brian Hines

title: Patriots 2026 scouting report for WR Kyle Dixon
summary: The New England Patriots decided to forgo the wide receiver position in this year’s NFL Draft, but they did sign a bunch of rookie free agents afterwards. Among that group, nobody had as unique a background as Kyle Dixon. A former baseball player in college, he spent his only two football seasons at Culver-Stockton in […]
full_text: Jul 28, 2026; Foxborough, MA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Kyle Dixon (83) runs after making a catch during training camp at Gillette Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Eric Canha-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots decided to forgo the wide receiver position in this year’s NFL Draft, but they did sign a bunch of rookie free agents afterwards. Among that group, nobody had as unique a background as Kyle Dixon. A former baseball player in college, he spent his only two football seasons at Culver-Stockton in the NAIA. Now, he is trying to leave his mark on the Patriots. Hard facts Name: Kyle Dixon Position: Wide receiver Jersey number: 83 Opening day age: 25 (9/14/2000) Measurements : 6’2 1/2”, 220 lbs, 9” hand size, 31 7/8” arm length, 78” wingspan, 4.50s 40-yard dash, 7.05s 3-cone drill, 4.51s short shuttle, 40 1/2” vertical jump, 10’11” broad jump, 15 bench press reps, 9.42 Relative Athletic Score Experience NFL: New England Patriots (2026-) | College: Southern Illinois Carbondale (2019-20), Southern Illinois Edwardsville (2021-22), Georgia Gwinnett (2023), Culver-Stockton (2024-25) Despite being of the most productive wide receivers in Illinois state history as well as an all-state defensive back as a junior, Dixon decided not to continue his football career beyond Carlinville, IL, High School. Instead, he opted for baseball entering college and ended up spending five years as a bullpen pitcher at various schools. In 2024, he made his return to a gridiron. It was a successful one. In just two seasons and 22 games with the NAIA’s Culver-Stockton Wildcats in Canton, MI, he caught 143 passes for 2,394 yards and 24 touchdowns. He also was voted first-team All-HAAC in both seasons. And yet, Dixon received only moderate interest entering the NFL and eventually went undrafted in 2026. He joined the Patriots as a rookie free agent shortly after hitting the market. Scouting report Strengths: Tall, lean, with broad shoulders and long limbs, Dixon very much looks the part of an NFL wide receiver — and not just that. He also offers decent straight-line speed and good leaping ability; he is well-suited to be competitive as a downfield receiver and competitive catch player both inside and on the perimeter. He transitions quickly from a receiver to a runner with the ball in his hands, and has shown the ability to break tackles to gain extra yards. His college production also was nothing short of impressive given his background. Weaknesses: There is no denying that Dixon’s game translating to the NFL is far from a given. Looking at his tape at Culver-Stockton, he mostly was the best athlete on the field and therefore at a clear advantage over his opposition. As far as his actual skillset is concerned, he is unsurprisingly raw throughout his route; his release technique, footwork at his break, and working back to the football are all a work in progress. He also is not the shiftiest receiver and more of a linear streaker but without the top-end speed to begin with. 2025 review Stats : 11 games | 83 catches, 1,282 receiving yards (15.4/catch), 12 TDs, 1 fumble (1 lost) | 1 carry, 5 rushing yards | 1-of-1, 11 passing yards Season recap: Typically in this section of our scouting reports, we provide some extra info that goes beyond the basic stats. However, this being Culver-Stockton we are talking about, there is limited information available about how Dixon fared statistically in 2025. What we do know is that he was once again pretty productive and finished the season as the Wildcats’ most productive pass catcher and one of the top performers in the NAIA. But just to paint the picture here. At Culver-Stockton, Dixon played in front of a crowd typically a fraction of what he is experiencing at your average Patriots training camp practice. The team’s highest recorded home attendance of 2025 was 945 spectators against St. Ambrose (IA). Dixon caught eight passes for 109 yards and a touchdown in that game. That was one of seven 100-yard games he had last season, but far from his top outing. A week later versus Central Methodist (MO), he recorded 11 catches for 236 yards and three scores — breaking a school record in receiving yards that had stood for 36 years and earning Heart Football Player of the Week honors. Unsurprisingly, Dixon was also named first-team All-HAAC for a second straight season. He also was later invited to participate in the Hula Bowl, where he hauled in four passes for 71 yards. 2026 preview Position: X-receiver | Ability: Camp body/Practice squad candidate | Contract: Signed through 2028 (2029 RFA) What will be his role? Dixon was used both outside and in the slot during his brief college football career, but based on his skillset projects mostly as an outside receiver at the next level. That said, the Patriots do like to cross-train their wideouts if they believe they can do so, meaning that a more flexible role could be in the cards as well especially given concerns about his ability to beat press-man coverage. Either way, Dixon is a package and backup player. What is his growth potential? Athletically, Dixon provides a decent ceiling. This, in turn, could help him develop into a usable depth piece on offense. Whether or not he can be anything more than that remains to be seen; the sample size thus far is simply too small and of an entirely different quality than what he will face as a pro. His potential for development is sizable, though. Does he have positional versatility? While not the most versatile of players, Dixon does have some attributes to his game that suggest he can be used as more than a one-trick pony. Training camp so far has already shown that: he has spent time with the returners, something he did not do in college. What is his salary cap situation? The Patriots signed him to a three-year undrafted rookie deal that came with sizable guarantees: a $17,000 signing bonus prorated over the length of the deal, plus $235,000 in salary guarantees for the 2026 season. As far as his cap impact is concerned, it consists of his $885,000 base salary plus that $5,833 signing bonus proration for a combined sum of $890,833. Under the Top 51 rule, only his guaranteed bonus counts against the cap in the offseason. How safe is his roster spot? Minimally. As an undrafted rookie receiver, Dixon was at a disadvantage to begin with; there is a reason he was not selected in the draft. So far this training camp, little has changed: he still remains near the bottom of the depth chart, with second-unit work the height of his success. Summary: Dixon has an intriguing skillset and after playing only two college seasons still has significant room for growth, particularly considering the massive jump in competition he is facing. That might be enough for him to be kept around on the practice squad, if his practice and preseason performance look the part as well. What do you think about Kyle Dixon heading into the 2026 season? Will he emerge from the depths of the roster? Will he maybe factor into the returner mix? Please head down to the comment section to share your thoughts.

summary: New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye described his wide receiver room by two words on Friday: crowded and competitive. The Patriots roster currently features seven wide receivers with NFL experience, as they acquired A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason to work with Kayshon Boutte, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - MAY 27: Efton Chism III #86 of the New England Patriots turns after a catch during New England Patriots OTA on May 27, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. Sportswire) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images New England Patriots quarterback Drake Maye described his wide receiver room by two words on Friday: crowded and competitive. The Patriots roster currently features seven wide receivers with NFL experience, as they acquired A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs this offseason to work with Kayshon Boutte, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, and Efton Chism III. As the roster must eventually dwindle down to 53 players, keeping all seven feels far fetched. That means at least one will be the odd man out. Among the group, Patriots fans view one as the clear odd man out. In the results of the latest SB Nation Reacts survey, 43% of participants said that was Efton Chism III . The comment section, however, was more split: Mosi_Tatupu Probably Chism gets cut but can’t rule out an aging Hollins or a trade for Boutte or injury, but as of right now it’s Chism on the bubble. Chu I put Chism because he may make it to PS and I think he redundant to Pop who I think is better underneath quick slot. Imagine McDaniels coming up with a wr version of Lil Woodhead. NittanyLions2.0: Boutte. I think he gets traded with his value increasing with his play. Hopefully he shows it in pre season. Might be able to get a fourth for him. 7i165 Hollins as he is in last year of his contract and could free 4m cap space. But only if other players show they are able to be as effective as him zionlion02 I’ll go wild card and say Demario. I think his play is too chaotic and uncontrolled and I’ve seen numerous mentions of him not being able to run routes. Boutte is a far better receiver playing a harder to replace role. mathblaster97 Cut Chism and stash him on the PS All in all, this week’s survey results look as follows: 21% of voters would prefer to keep all seven, with multiple participants noting the depth would be welcomed for injury insurance. DeMario Douglas, who enters the final year of his rookie contract, was the next receiver to be listed receiving 15% of the votes. Despite potentially being the most likely to be the odd man out after a trade request this past spring entering the last year of his contract, Kayshon Boutte received the least amount of votes at 4%. No matter who is on the outside-looking-in come Week 1, New England is hoping the improvements atop the wide receiver depth chart will help them get back to the Super Bowl and finish the job this time, as they currently have the eighth highest odds on FanDuel Sportsbook to win Super Bowl LXI — the fifth highest odds in the AFC.

title: Saints LB Pete Werner speaks on leadership after Demario Davis’ departure
summary: Demario Davis signing back with the New York Jets this summer no doubt leaves a huge void in the Saints locker room, not only for his play but for his commanding leadership. Speaking to the media after day 3 of camp, linebacker Pete Werner touched on what he learned from playing alongside Davis and how […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 23 : Pete Werner #20 of the New Orleans Saints looks on from the field during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Caesars Superdome on November 23, 2025 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images Demario Davis signing back with the New York Jets this summer no doubt leaves a huge void in the Saints locker room, not only for his play but for his commanding leadership. Speaking to the media after day 3 of camp, linebacker Pete Werner touched on what he learned from playing alongside Davis and how his own leadership style has developed over his five years in the NFL. "Being in this system, you start to develop a voice and you want to be a guy that the guys can rely on." Pete Werner says that he's always been a "lead by example" type of leader but his style of leadership has changed to being more vocal. He mentions playing w/ Demario Davis. pic.twitter.com/GbXsXsQSMz — Meagan Glover (@MeaganGTV) July 31, 2026 “Second year in the [Brandon] Staley defense, you start to develop a little confidence,” said Werner. The former Ohio State Buckeye mentioned his excitement to be reunited with Kaden Elliss, who returns to New Orleans after three seasons in Atlanta, but also made a point about the departing vet. “We miss a guy like Demario; that’s gonna be a guy that’s hard to replace.” “I’ve always been a guy that’s, you know, lead by example,” said Werner. “But being in this system, you start to develop a voice, and you want to be a guy that the guys can rely on. And I see myself in that position, not only making plays on the field but helping guys off the field and uniting this defense together.” With Davis’ exit, the linebacker room has lost its leader. Werner embracing the challenge of stewardship among his peers could go a long way toward replacing Davis’ outsized impact. Tell us your outlook for Pete Werner entering year six?

title: The culture is beginning to show for the Saints
summary: Throughout all of last training camp, there were questions everywhere. Questions about how Kellen Moore would schedule practices, how the team would handle the heat, why they had so many rest days, and who would be the starting quarterback. But by the end of the season, those questions began to fade away and as the […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 30: Head coach Kellen Moore of the New Orleans Saints attends training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 30, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Throughout all of last training camp, there were questions everywhere. Questions about how Kellen Moore would schedule practices, how the team would handle the heat, why they had so many rest days, and who would be the starting quarterback. But by the end of the season, those questions began to fade away and as the questions disappeared, a culture started to take shape. For the first time since Sean Payton left the sidelines, the locker room feels close. The team may not have a fully defined identity yet, but they do have a culture. What does it mean for a football team to have a culture? Culture is the shared attitude, work ethic, and commitment to a common goal. In order to become a true team, a group of individuals has to put pride and egos aside and embrace the expectation that the group’s success comes before individual recognition. Culture is Spencer Rattler taking a backseat to Tyler Shough, being excited to watch him grow and thrive, while still preparing himself in case the team needs him. Culture is Chris Olave showing up to training camp and participating in portions of practice while negotiating his new contract. Culture is Chase Young emerging as a vocal leader in the locker room, mentoring the younger defensive linemen and helping the entire defense improve. Culture is Alvin Kamara entering the season excited to play and remain a Saint. It’s much easier for a culture to take shape when the leadership has a clear vision and a plan that has already produced success. While that success has been limited, it has been enough for the players to buy into the process. Every player in this organization is preaching a team-first mentality and doing their part to elevate the team because they got a taste of success as last season came to a close and watched this team continue to grow. Justin Reid spoke with the media following Wednesday’s practice and spent much of his time at the podium talking about his teammates and giving credit to the other players in the defensive back room. That is culture personified. "Kool-Aid McKinstry is a baller," – @JustinqReid pic.twitter.com/DoZyspNUe9 — New Orleans Saints (@Saints) July 29, 2026 Before a team can establish an identity, it first has to come together and this team is beginning to do exactly that. They are laying the foundation for something very special. Have you noticed a change in the attitude of the players and does it make you excited about where the direction of this team is headed?

title: NY Giants training camp report, practice 4: Winners, losers, more takeaways
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — On the fourth day of 2026 training camp, New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh believes the team took “a good step” in a positive direction. The Giants get their first off day of camp on Sunday, after which they will practice for six straight days before heading back to […]
full_text: John Harbaugh | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — On the fourth day of 2026 training camp, New York Giants head coach John Harbaugh believes the team took “a good step” in a positive direction. The Giants get their first off day of camp on Sunday, after which they will practice for six straight days before heading back to East Rutherford, N.J. So, this was an appropriate time to ask the coach for an assessment of what has taken place thus far. “You don’t really measure too much. You just try to do as good as you can at everything you can,” Harbaugh said. “I felt like today was a good step because a lot of the things that we were working on from yesterday and the first couple of days, we saw the improvement today in terms of execution. “So that’s what you really want to see is better today than you were yesterday. It’s kind of the measuring stick. I felt like we did that today.” Harbaugh was particularly pleased with the offense, which had only one false start on Saturday after a rash of them over the first three practices. “The operation was better on offense, for sure,” Harbaugh said. “We’re pushing the envelope on all the cadences. “It’s not like we’re protecting it and going simple cadences. There was a lot of tough cadences, and for the most part, we did a really good job of it.” Let’s get to the rest of what we saw on Saturday. Winners Odell Beckham fans — For three days, fans have come to the Greenbrier hoping for an Odell Beckham highlight. He finally provided one on Saturday, leaping to snag a touchdown pass of roughly 25 yards from Jameis Winston Winston. Theo Johnson — The third-year tight end, who has seemingly always struggled with catching the ball consistently, had a really good day. He made several nice catches. The best might have been a deep catch on a ball feathered beautifully over cornerback Jarrick Bernard-Converse by Jaxson Dart. Johnson dropped easy passes in each of the first two practices, so this was nice to see. Tanner Conner — I don’t know if Conner, a tight end who came to the Giants late last season, can make the roster. I have to add him here because he has been productive every day catching passes from Jameis Winston. He had at least four catches on Saturday, all from Winston. Chris Manhertz — Yep, another tight end. The veteran blocking tight end has four catches in two seasons with the Giants. He had three, and nearly came down with a fourth, on Saturday. So, he has met his quota. Dominic Zvada — It was the rookie placekicker’s turn to kick field goals on Saturday, and he made the most of it. Zvada made 13 of 14 kicks, including a couple in late-game “must-score” situations where the offense was trailing. He made a couple of kicks from roughly 51 yards. The Greenbrier East and Greenbrier West high school football teams — Both teams attended the practice and were brought down to the field afterward, where they were presented with a $5,000 check on behalf of the Giants. The pass rush — I can’t try to count “sacks” during these practices. They aren’t real, and the quarterbacks never get touched. but, what was clear is that Jaxson Dart and Winston were rarely able to just set their feet and throw comfortably. Paulson Adebo (with an assist from Tremaine Edmunds) — Over the first few days of practice, Giants defensive backs had their hands on several passes. They could not, though, reel any of them in for interceptions. That changed Saturday. After linebacker Tremaine Edmunds tipped a Dart pass at the line of scrimmage, Adebo snagged it and took for a touchdown. Tremaine Edmunds — Edmunds created the Adebo interception. He also had one himself. Dart tried to float a pass over the backpedaling Edmunds, who is nearly 6-foot-5 and has a 97th percentile wing span. Edmunds wasn’t having, reaching up to intercept the ball. When the Giants drafted Arvell Reese, who is also 6-4, to play alongside Edmunds, they talked about the space that duo would take up and how difficult they would make it for quarterbacks to complete passes in windows tightened by their size. We have seen that come to fruition a number of times over the first four practices. Jack Kelly — The rookie linebacker, a sixth-round pick, made a pair of nice plays. During a 7-on-7 drill, he jumped a crossing route intended for Isaiah Likely and knocked it away. During 11-on-11, he showed tremendous range by knocking away a deep ball from Dart that was intended for speedy wide receiver Calvin Austin. Losers Colton Hood — Honestly, I’m reaching for a loser here. Hood is only a “loser” because an offside penalty on a defensive lineman cost Hood a pick six. The rookie cornerback intercepted a Winston pass and took it to the house, but it didn’t count. So, he “lost” a pick six. Trivia participants — Let’s just say these Giants fans struggled with their history. John Mara attends practice The Giants’ co-owner attended practice on Saturday for the second time in four days. Below, Mara, who has been battling cancer, walks off the field with head coach John Harbaugh and GM Joe Schoen. John Mara, John Harbaugh and Joe Schoen leave the practice field at the end of Day 4 at Giants camp on Saturday. (Oh, and Jerry Meade). pic.twitter.com/z1ywzoX5Cs — Art Stapleton (@art_stapleton) August 1, 2026 Malik Nabers practices Malik Nabers was back at practice on Saturday after having an off day on Friday as he recovers from a torn ACL. Early on, it did not look like Nabers would practice. He had a baseball cap on and did not initially warm up. He did, though, participate in the limited fashion which is becoming customary. Malik Nabers was back on the practice field after being off on Saturday. He watched the early portion of indy drills before running a handful of routes and participating in a jog-through install period. pic.twitter.com/H8TWSdRnyT — Dan Duggan (@DDuggan21) August 1, 2026 Full pads on Monday Things get real on Monday when the Giants return to practice. They will be in full pads for the first time, Harbaugh said on Saturday. “We’re not going to be tackling to the ground,” Harbaugh said. “But we’ll be in what we call wrap and release. So we’re trying to stop the ball carrier if we can in defense. Pads behind us on offense, things like that. “I’m sure inside it’ll be a little more physical than it is out here without the shoulder pads. So it just ramps up just a little bit. But other than that, everything will be exactly the same.” Something to watch Despite Harbaugh’s reminders to keep players on their feet, tight end Isaiah Likely was slammed to the ground after catching a pass during a “must-score” situation late in practice. Likely got up slowly. We will have to wait until Monday to see if Likely suffered any ill-effects. Remaining Greenbrier practice schedule Sunday, August 2 — Players’ day off Monday, August 3 — 1:30-3:15 p.m. Tuesday, August 4 — 1:30-3:30 p.m. Wednesday, August 5 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Thursday, August 6 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Friday, August 7 — 1:30-4 p.m. (Open to the public) Saturday, August 8 — 10 a.m. – 12:30 p.m.

title: NY Giants training camp, practice No. 4: Discussion, news, updates
summary: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants will return to the Greenbrier Sports Performance Center practice field for their fourth training camp practice on Saturday at 1:30 p.m. ET. This will be an unpadded two-hour workout. The Giants will get their only off day of their West Virginia trip on Sunday. That will […]
full_text: WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — The New York Giants will return to the Greenbrier Sports Performance Center practice field for their fourth training camp practice on Saturday at 1:30 p.m. ET. This will be an unpadded two-hour workout. The Giants will get their only off day of their West Virginia trip on Sunday. title: Survey results: The defense and Dart have the fans’ attention
summary: The New York Giants 2026 training camp is under way, and it’s already been a lively one. We expected a “Harbaugh” camp to be different from what we’ve seen from the Giants in recent years, with free agent tight end Isaiah Likely warning his new teammates to expect a tough environment. And despite the gorgeous […]
full_text: New York Giants pass rusher Abdul Carter after a play | Getty Images The New York Giants 2026 training camp is under way, and it’s already been a lively one. We expected a “Harbaugh” camp to be different from what we’ve seen from the Giants in recent years, with free agent tight end Isaiah Likely warning his new teammates to expect a tough environment. And despite the gorgeous views at Greenbrier, John Harbaugh’s first camp has been, active, competitive, and hard. Even so, we weren’t quite sure what to expect from this year’s camp with a new coaching staff, renovated roster, and a new venue. So for this week’s survey we asked fans what they were most interested in as camp opened, Perhaps unsurprisingly, most fans pointed to the defense and Jaxson Dart. The defense just edged out Dart in our poll, and they’re also some of the biggest storylines through the first three practices of camp. The offense won the first practice of camp, with Dart looking good as he delivered accurate passes and layered the ball over defenders in the intermediate area. Videos from camp have shown Dart throwing with more solid and repeatable technique, featuring crisp footwork, a solid foundation, and a slightly more compact three-quarters release. That should allow him to be more consistently accurate as well as better able to drive the ball. The defense, however, took over on the second and third days of camp. The secondary got their hands on at least four passes in the second practice — though they couldn’t haul in any of the potential interceptions. The defensive front has been the star of the show, disrupting the offense at every opportunity. Second year edge defender, in particular, has been an absolute menace. He’s been credited with at least four sacks through the last two practices and has given All-Pro left tackle Andrew Thomas all he can handle. Carter said after Friday’s practice that he’s set a goal of becoming Defensive Player Of the Year, and believes he can do so as soon as this season. Right now, Vegas disagrees giving him just the 13th-best odds of being named DPOY at +4,000 ( per FanDuel ), trailing Brian Burns at 12th (+3,300). We might see those odds shorten if both pass rushers can keep building on their performances in camp. The rest of the front has shown out too, with Kayvon Thibodeaux disrupting behind the line of scrimmage, getting sacks and flushing the quarterback into his teammates’ arms, batting down passes, and even tipping one to himself for a pick six. Even second year defensive tackle Darius Alexander came away with an interception in the play of the day on Friday. The Giants’ defense was a major pain point for fans in 2024 and 2025, but the early indications are that Dennard Wilson’s unit could be a lot of fun to watch in 2026. They’re also providing great work Dart as he continues to improve.
author: Chris Pflum

title: NY Giants Abdul Carter sets lofty goal for second NFL season
summary: The New York Giants are hoping for, and expecting, big things from edge defender Abdul Carter as he enters his second year. The team is expecting that he’ll live up to his athletic potential after a disappointing rookie season. The Giants are hoping that Carter can become the kind of impact player they envisioned when […]
full_text: Abdul Carter | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The New York Giants are hoping for, and expecting, big things from edge defender Abdul Carter as he enters his second year. The team is expecting that he’ll live up to his athletic potential after a disappointing rookie season. The Giants are hoping that Carter can become the kind of impact player they envisioned when selecting him with the third overall pick in the 2025 NFL Draft. For his part, Carter has his sights set just a bit higher than being an impact player on defense. He wants to be, and believes he can be, the best defender in the NFL. “I want to be Defensive Player of the Year,” Carter said, when asked about his goals. This isn’t some far-off goal for Carter, either. He believes he can do it. “Absolutely,” he said. “I know what I’m capable of. I know if I put the work in and believe in myself, trust in myself, trust in my teammates, trust in my coaching, I can be whoever I want to be.” If the first three days of training camp are any indication, Carter is at the very least a problem for opposing offensive linemen. He was credited with multiple sacks on Thursday and followed that up with at least one more on Friday. Carter has been a consistent presence in the offensive backfield, and a highly disruptive force behind the line of scrimmage. In a change from his rookie camp, Carter has been primarily working on the defensive right, over the left tackle. He insists that he’ll be moving around as camp progresses, saying, “I’m in one spot right now, but I’m still going to be moving around. I’m going to be over the guards, be over the centers. It’s going to be fun.” But for now the coaches seem to be controlling variables for Carter, only sending him against the left tackle. But he also isn’t rushing against just any left tackle, he’s rushing against one of the NFL’s best in Andrew Thomas. The battles between the two have been some of the highlights of camp over the first three days. For his part, Thomas has complimented both Carter’s athletic prowess as well as his improvement since last season. “He can work edges really well,” Thomas said on Thursday. “Part of that is that he’s not a super tall rusher. He’s bending down with good ankle flexion. He’s really low to the ground, but he also has a good change of direction, so you can’t just anticipate which way he’s going to go, because he can cut off both feet. “He’s stringing his moves together better. He’s using his power more, and you can tell he just has a better understanding for different types of blocks, different types of attacks, recognizing play schemes.” For his part, Carter is grateful to go against a great left tackle who will push him to excel. “I’m still growing,” Carter said. “But it means a lot coming from him [Thomas], especially the guys he’s been against, how long he’s been doing that at a high level. “Andrew, he’s the best of the best. Whenever we’re going against each other, we get the most out of each other. If I beat him, I’m going to let him hear about it, but he’s the best of the best.” Carter has gotten the better of Thomas several times so far. Though, in fairness to both players, pads haven’t gone on yet, which does give the pass rusher a distinct advantage. But, as the saying goes, “To be the best, you’ve got to beat the best.” It follows then, that practicing against, and beating, one of the best left tackles in the NFL is a good first step if Carter wants to achieve his goal of being the Defensive Player of the Year.
author: Chris Pflum

title: New York Giants mailbag: Jon Runyan, power rankings, draft picks, more questions
summary: Norm Weiss asks: Ed, in your roster projection article you listed Jon Runyan in the “bubble” category. I understand with a $9.25M cap savings and the fact that he doesn’t appear to fit the mold of the mauling inter OL player that Coach Harbaugh wants, but there doesn’t appear to be any enticing options on […]
full_text: Norm Weiss asks: Ed, in your roster projection article you listed Jon Runyan in the “bubble” category. I understand with a $9.25M cap savings and the fact that he doesn’t appear to fit the mold of the mauling inter OL player that Coach Harbaugh wants, but there doesn’t appear to be any enticing options on the current roster. I know it’s highly speculative, do you believe there are any veteran LG options that are likely to become available from other rosters who would provide cap relief and better fit the mold of a mauling interior lineman? Ed says: Norm, I don’t know who will become available. If the Giants move on from Runyan, and I did not see any evidence from spring practices that they are considering doing that, it will be because they believe they already have a replacement on the roster. The first few practices of training camp have also not given any indication that Runyan could be in jeopardy. The most likely 2026 replacement would be Daniel Faalele. He started at right guard for Harbaugh with the Baltimore Ravens the past two seasons, and spent the spring working at both guard spots. He was the only player to take any first-team reps at left guard other than Runyan, and that was just a few. Philip Green asks: Who is competing to back up JMS at center? I was actually hoping that (Austin) Schlottman would compete to be the starter (without any stats, I thought our running game was better when he started last year), but we lost him to the Titans. I’m very happy with Mbow as the swing tackle and I think Neal and Faalele will have a pretty good competition with Runyan for the left guard spot, but I don’t have any idea what’s going to happen at center. Ed says: Philip, Lucas Patrick and Bryan Hudson are the players competing to back up John Michael Schmitz. Patrick is a 33-year-old entering his 10th NFL season. He has played in 113 regular-season games, with 65 starts. He has experience at center and both guard spots. Hudson is a 25-year-old former undrafted free agent who has been on the Giants’ practice squad since laste in the 2024 season. I would think Patrick is the favorite, but won’t be shocked in Hudson wins the job. James Carley asks: You and your team have discussed the dynamics of having Nagy, Callahan, and Roman on offense. There hasn’t been much, if any, discussion about the defensive side. BBV has provided comparisons of current D players success/failure under Bowen and Wink, but I haven’t seen comparisons to their work under Bullen, which was definitely a vast improvement. Harbaugh thought enough of him to keep him on the staff, and the players certainly seemed to like him. How will CB impact the defensive scheme and player decisions, and will Wilson partner with him the way Nagy has talked about Callahan and Roman? Do you think that as the D goes this year, so go the Giants? Ed says: James, I don’t believe the defense is set up the same way as the offense. Nagy, Callahan, and Roman have different strengths that complement each other. They all bring something to the table, and Nagy puts the pieces together. The defense is Dennard Wilson’s show. Now, I’m sure he has relied on Bullen to help him learn about certain players. I’m sure he is open to suggestions. I think, though, that Wilson was brought in by Harbaugh to run defense the way it was done in Baltimore. I’m sure Wilson has relied on Bullen to give him information on players, and that the entire defensive staff discusses ideas. I don’t, though, think the dynamic among defensive coaches is the same as it is on offense. Maybe a year from now Bullen gets to coordinate his own defense. Peter Smyth asks: I was very offended by the 7/28 Athletics Power Rankings putting the G-men at #28. The reporting seemed cookie cutter and out of date. I’m not asking you to trash a fellow journalist, but how can anyone seriously think we are only slightly better than the very worst teams in the NFL! My question: Is this a sign that the national media is far more skeptical of the Giants than people closer to the team? And if this is the case, where would you rank the team? Even a ballpark would be helpful. Am I just a Pollyanna-pre-training-camp-fanboy who thinks the team should be ranked in the middle at least? God help us all if we finish 28th! Ed says: Peter, they are just meaningless pre-training camp power rankings. Relax a little. That said, I was also surprised The Athletic had the Giants that low. We posted a summary of power rankings and the rest had the Giants in the 21-24 range. I think that is fair considering that while the Giants are expected to be better, they have to prove how much better. Bob Donnelly asks: It’s been said that good teams are built through the draft, especially players selected in the first three rounds. There’s also the notion of players being a good fit for the coaching philosophy. Schoen has drafted 14 players in the first three rounds for the prior coaching staff, 11 of which are currently on the roster, some of whom have not played up to expectations. As we head into training camp which of the 11 do you view as a good fit for this coaching staff? Looking at the ones that have yet to meet expectations are there any you believe will blossom under the new leadership? How many of the 11 do you see on the ‘27 roster? Ed says: Bob, let’s quickly go through all 11. Edge Kayvon Thibodeaux — Hasn’t lived up to his status as the No. 5 overall pick in 2022, but he is a good fit in any defense. He can go forward, backward, is an excellent run defender, and a good but not great pass rusher. Honestly, I think Thibodeaux might be headed for an outstanding year. Guard Evan Neal — Has the massive body that John Harbaugh loves in interior offensive linemen. He is still working with the third team, meaning he barely gets on the field in practice. A longshot to make the team. Tackle Josh Ezeudu — Right now, Ezeudu takes second-team reps at right tackle with Marcus Mbow on the left. He has position flex. Offensive line coach Mike Bloomgren seems to like him. He has a chance to stick. Cornerback Deonte Banks — Dennard Wilson’s scheme asks cornerbacks to play more aggressively than Shane Bowen’s did. That suits Banks. He is making the team. Center John Michael Schmitz — He is, and will be, the 2026 starting center. The question will come after the season when his rookie contract expires. Will Harbaugh see him as the answer long-term, or will he want a more physically imposing player at the position? Wide receiver Jalin Hyatt — I will be stunned if he makes this team. That’s all. Wide receiver Malik Nabers — He fits any team. Do I need to say more? Safety Tyler Nubin — He is smart and aggressive, and is still working with the first-team defense. He needs to make more plays, though. It won’t shock me if Ar’Darius Washington or Jason Pinnock steals his starting job. Nickel cornerback Dru Phillips — Honestly, I think Wilson and Harbaugh are going to love Phillips. He is an aggressive run defender and physical player. Edge Abdul Carter — I believe Carter really could have benefitted from Harbaugh as a rookie. I was told by multiple draft analysts NFL teams knew he had some maturity issues entering the league and needed to have a solid plan to guide him put in place. The Giants didn’t have one, and we know how it went. Carter is going to have a big year. Quarterback Jaxson Dart — I couldn’t tell you if Harbaugh would have banged the table to draft Dart the way Brian Daboll did. I do know that Dart’s presence is one of the big reasons Harbaugh took the Giants’ job. Dave Prenske asks: There has been a lot written and discussed about Shane Bowen’s scheme and its lack of fit to the Giants’ personnel. Can you speak to what Bowen’s system was trying to do and what kinds of players would thrive in it? Are there examples of teams that run it or something similar successfully? title: Ex-Jets Progress Report: Part 1 (NFC)
summary: With training camp underway, it’s a good time to keep track of where any former Jets are currently playing, so we can start to access how likely they are to have successful seasons elsewhere, or to lose their jobs and potentially become available for a reunion with the Jets. We will cover this over two […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MARYLAND - DECEMBER 25: Quinnen Williams #92 of the Dallas Cowboys blocks against the Washington Commanders at Northwest Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by G Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images With training camp underway, it’s a good time to keep track of where any former Jets are currently playing, so we can start to access how likely they are to have successful seasons elsewhere, or to lose their jobs and potentially become available for a reunion with the Jets. We will cover this over two parts, looking at NFC teams today and AFC teams next week. Every NFC team currently has at least two former Jets on it. As ever, this list is intended to be exhaustive, but if we missed anyone, let us know in the comments. Commanders: The biggest names for Washington are linebacker Frankie Luvu and defensive tackle Javon Kinlaw , each of whom are on big-money deals but had disappointing seasons in 2025. Luvu was a second-team all-pro in 2024. Tight end Lawrence Cager is also on the roster, having signed a futures deal, but Anthony Firkser was recently released and linebacker Nick Bellore just retired. Cowboys: Dallas obviously has Quinnen Williams among their ranks following last season’s blockbuster trade. However, he’s been joined by a handful of familiar faces on the other side of the ball. Running back Israel Abanikanda signed a futures deal after the season and was subsequently joined by offensive lineman Chris Glaser and wideout Denzel Mims . Dallas also signed wideout Tyler Johnson in free agency and he’ll be hoping for a bounce-back year. Eagles: Punter Braden Mann and defensive back Michael Carter II remain with the Eagles, although Carter unsurprisingly took a major paycut to remain with them. Mann has established himself as one of the league’s better punters since leaving the Jets. Tight end EJ Jenkins returned on a futures deal and the Eagles opted to take a flyer on wide receiver Elijah Moore , who was most recently in Denver. Giants: The Giants have loaded up on ex-Jets since the middle of last year, although most of them look like being role players at best. Safety Jason Pinnock , making his return to the Giants, might have the best shot at starting. At wide receiver, New York retained Xavier Gipson after picking him up last year and another ex-Jet Braxton Berrios will compete with him both in terms of receiver roles and in the return game. Two ex-Jets, Shelby Harris and Leki Fotu , were recently signed as a reaction to Roy Robertson-Harris tearing his Achilles and will now compete for a defensive tackle role. Linebacker Zaire Barnes was re-signed and will try to earn a role on defense along with three former Jets defensive backs: Korie Black , Jarrick Bernard-Converse and Elijah Campbell . Packers: One recent Jet who could be a key reserve for a Packers in 2026 is quarterback Tyrod Taylor . Their other three ex-Jets are long-shots with defensive backs Jaylin Simpson and Shemar Bartholomew being joined by recent signing Lenny Krieg at placekicker. Vikings: The Vikings recently signed former Jets safety Jamal Adams , but he’ll be competing for a role at inside linebacker. One of the names ahead of him is another former Jet, starter Blake Cashman . Bears: Chicago already had ex-Jets kicker Cairo Santos on their team but the addition of wide receiver Kalif Raymond should further strengthen their special teams unit in the return game. Lions: Having lost Raymond to their divisional rivals, the Lions replaced him with another former Jet receiver and return man, Greg Dortch . He has a good chance to make a team that will also feature former Jets cornerback DJ Reed on defense. Safety Chuck Clark will compete for a role in the secondary alongside Reed, while quarterback Teddy Bridgewater and wide receiver Tarik Black were also added to compete for a role. Bucs: Guard Dan Feeney saw his contract expire at the end of last season, but he was re-signed. The Bucs also retained former Jets kicker Chase McLaughlin . Saints: Although Demario Davis returned to the Jets, the Saints still have one key ex-Jets player contributing on defense in defensive tackle Nathan Shepherd . Their only other former Jet is quarterback Zach Wilson , who is on his third team in three years since leaving the Jets. Panthers: Carolina signed former Jets receiver John Metchie III during free agency. They also have Claud Cherelus returning at linebacker, but another ex-Jets linebacker – Jared Bartlett – was recently waived. Falcons: Atlanta signed kicker Nick Folk , who beat them on a long last second kick in a 2025 game, during free agency. The only other ex-Jet on the team is Corey Levin , who will compete for a backup role on the interior offensive line. Rams: Wide receiver Davante Adams caught 14 touchdown passes last year and will once again have a role on a team that could be one of the favorites to win the Super Bowl. Another ex-Jet, Harrison Mevis , looks secure in his role, as the Rams don’t have another kicker on the roster. Seahawks: The Super Bowl champions will look to repeat with ex-Jets quarterback Sam Darnold at the helm and defensive tackle Leonard Williams once again spearheading the defense. The special teams unit has a bunch of ex-Jets playing key roles as Jason Myers is still the kicker and Chazz Surratt , Irv Charles and JaMarkis Weston should all contribute in kick coverage. Cardinals: Arizona opens camp in 2026 with three ex-Jets on their roster: Running back Bam Knight , defensive back Isaiah Oliver and tight end Kenny Yeboah . Of the three, Oliver perhaps has the most likely chance of earning a significant role. 49ers: Finally, the 49ers still have Eddy Pineiro as their kicker, again with nobody in camp to compete with him. Safety Ashtyn Davis will also be expecting to make the roster. Quarterback Adrian Martinez is also back, after signing a futures deal. Defensive end Bryce Huff retired and linebacker Milo Eifler was recently released. We’ll be back with a rundown of which AFC teams have ex-Jets among their ranks in a few days…

While nominally he competed with Joe Tippmann for the starting center job, Tippmann was widely expected to take the role. Things changed a few days before the start of the regular season when Alijah Vera-Tucker suffered a season ending triceps injury. Myers was inserted into the starting lineup of a reshuffled offensive line. To the extent there are metrics that rank interior offensive lineman, most graded Myers as a low tier starter. His play was at least stable enough to help the Jets have a middle of the pack offensive line, and he was rewarded with a 2 year, $11 million contract before the end of the season. 2026 will be a success if: Myers plays well enough that the Jets feel secure with him as the starter for 2027. His contract isn’t cheap. He is making mid-tier money for a starting center. But the Jets can move on from his contract painlessly after the season so the pressure is on Myers to play effective football. Odds of making the roster: Lock (>99%)
