title: Eagles Training Camp Practice Notes: Jalyx Hunt and Jalen Carter help defense win the day
summary: Today marked the third Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. The non-padded session lasted for a tad shy of two hours. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex. EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES UP NEXT: The Eagles have a rest day on Sunday before returning to practice on Monday […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 4: Jalyx Hunt #58 of the Philadelphia Eagles looks on against the Washington Commanders at Lincoln Financial Field on January 4, 2026 in Philadelphia, United States. (Photo by Mitchell Leff/Getty Images) | Getty Images Today marked the third Philadelphia Eagles training camp practice ahead of the 2026 NFL season. The non-padded session lasted for a tad shy of two hours. Here’s what I observed at the Jefferson Health Training Complex. EAGLES PRACTICE NOTES JALEN HURTS UPDATE: More bad than good from Hurts and the offense in this practice. THE GOOD: Hurts floated a pass to DeVonta Smith along the left sideline for about 15 yards on an extended play (though he may have been “sacked” before getting the throw off). Hurts ripped a throw over the middle to Britain Covey in a tight window. The ball was bobbled and nearly picked off but that wasn’t Hurts’ fault. I liked the aggression from the Eagles’ QB. Hurts made a good completion to a crossing Covey in 7-on-7 with Quinyon Mitchell trailing in the area. During situational drills late in practice, Hurts hit Dontayvion Wicks — who was going up against Michael Carter II — in stride on a quick slant to pick up a crucial first down. THE BAD: Early in the first 11-on-11 series, Hurts threw two passes that were batted down at the line of scrimmage. Hurts couldn’t drop a pass to Dallas Goedert in the bucket, instead overthrowing his tight end. Hurts took a lot of “sacks.” A lot. SportsRadio 94WIP’s Eliot Shorr-Parks charted eight of them. Some were a result of quick pressure but others were a result of him holding onto the ball for a long time. After the first day of practice , I talked about how under center play-action can help Hurts’ timing in the passing game. Well, there didn’t seem to be as much of that today with the Eagles more commonly operating out of the shotgun. Hurts threw a checkdown to Saquon Barkley that got knocked down by Jeremiah Trotter Jr. Hurts overshot a downfield target to Makai Lemon, though I wonder if the rookie failed to properly get to his spot. The offense generally struggled to move the ball. THE BOTTOM LINE BECAUSE STONE COLD SAID SO: Day 1 featured encouraging signs from Hurts. Day 2 and Day 3 served to remind us that the offense is still very much a work in progress. EAGLES INJURY UPDATES: BGN’s Alexis Chassen wrote in more detail about the Eagles’ injury situation . An overview below: DID NOT PRACTICE: OT Lane Johnson (excused absence/not injury related) LB Jihaad Campbell (excused absence/not injury related) DT Ta’Quon Graham (excused absence/not injury related) WR Elijah Moore (excused absence/not injury related) OT Cameron Williams (knee contusion) S Cole Wisniewski (hamstring) IN-PRACTICE INJURIES: OG Micah Morris and EDGE Keyshawn James-Newby left practice early to visit the medical tent. Undrafted rookie OL Jaedan Roberts was carted off after going down with what appeared to be a serious injury on the final play of practice. Pretty unfortunate. DEFENSE DOMINATES: Buy all the Jalyx Hunt stock you can possibly acquire. The third-year edge rusher has been on fire to start camp. Hunt took advantage of Lane Johnson’s absence by terrorizing Fred Johnson, who repped at first-team right tackle. Hunt was living in the backfield both against the run and the pass. I also believe I saw him deflect a pass at the line of scrimmage. Jalen Carter has also started camp strong. Fresh off a record-breaking contract extension , Carter has been putting in the work on the field. He knocked down a Hurts pass at the line of scrimmage and also “sacked” a quarterback on a play where edge rush pressure forced Hurts to step up into Carter’s waiting embrace. No Jihaad Campbell? No problem. Jeremiah Trotter Jr. took advantage of his reps with the first-team defense. Trot Jr. was in position to blow up Tank Bigsby in the flat right after the running back caught a pass from Hurts. Trot Jr. broke up a pass on a play where Hurts first read the field right and then turned left to try to throw a dump off to Barkley only for the ball to be knocked down. Good range and discipline from the Eagles’ third-year linebacker. If Campbell and/or Zack Baun have to miss time this season, I feel good about Trot Jr. being able to fill the void. SLOW START FOR THE EAGLES’ TOP TWO DRAFT PICKS: All the necessary disclaimers apply here. Rookie players, only the third day of camp, no pads yet, new offense going up against an established defense, yada yada yada. So, we’re in a safe space now, right? No one is going to overreact to what I’m about to share? Okay, good … because it’s been a quiet start to camp for Makai Lemon and Eli Stowers. (gasp) I’ve yet to see any kind of “wow” factor with Lemon. He didn’t look very fast on a vertical target where the ball landed in front of him. Not sure if that incompletion was an overthrow or if he simply didn’t get to where Hurts was expecting him to be. Lemon failed to hold on to the football on a target over the middle where Andrew Mukuba bumped him from behind as he was trying to make the catch. Lemon did draw either a defensive pass interference or defensive holding penalty during a red zone sequence, which is good! But his route on that play didn’t look very crisp prior to the contact. Lemon has looked natural fielding punts, which I didn’t fully expect since he only returned six of those in college. That’s been good to see. Ultimately, I think the Eagles are putting Lemon in a tough spot as a rookie. They really need him to be ready to contribute in a significant way as a rookie. To this point, I’m not ready to say I feel good about his chances in that regard. Of course, plenty of time for that to change between now and Week 1. Stowers was pretty invisible during spring drills and he hasn’t done much to impress in the summer so far, either. The rookie tight end did do a nice job of playing defense and breaking up an off-target Tanner McKee pass that was put into harm’s way. But then another McKee throw hit him in the hands and he couldn’t make the grab while being covered by Mac McWilliams. Dontayvion Wicks looks like a solid starting wide receiver so far. Don’t sleep on my guy Darius Cooper. Last year’s unexpected summer standout continues to make catches in camp. His most impressive snag came on a play where Hurts placed the ball a tad high but Cooper caught it above his head. Cooper has seen a decent share of first-team reps … and certainly more than Johnny Wilson, which seems notable since Nick Sirianni grouped those two in the same bucket competing for a “dirty work” role. Speaking of Wilson, he had a catch knocked out of his hands by Jakorian Bennett. Probably an incompletion and not a fumble but a play that should’ve been made all the same. Speaking of Bennett, he was flagged for DPI on a play where he basically tackled Quez Watkins well before the ball arrived. BACKUP QUARTERBACK BATTLE: Judging on camp alone, I’d give the edge to Andy Dalton over Tanner McKee thus far. Dalton has had more fruitful completions. Some nice plays by the Eagles’ safeties. As I already mentioned, Mukuba helped to break up a Hurts pass to Lemon in 7-on-7. The second-year safety read the quarterback and broke on the ball to force the incompletion. Marcus Epps had good downfield coverage on Goedert during the aforementioned play where Hurts overthrew his tight end. Jordan Davis had a nice rep where he played the run (Saquon Barkley on play-action) before pursuing Hurts and pressuring the quarterback into a run for short gain/no gain to the left side. Drew Kendall saw some first-team left guard action with Landon Dickerson not taking 100% of the reps with the starters. The second-team offensive line today: LT Markel Bell, LG Jake Majors, C Drew Kendall, RG Micah Morris (prior to injury), RT John Ojukwu. Majors had previously seen second-team center action. On Thursday, I mentioned how I was curious to see Payton’s response to a bad Day 2. It was good to see the…

title: Landon Dickerson denies retirement rumors
summary: The Eagles had a lot of questions surrounding their offensive line in the months following the end of the 2025 season, but Landon Dickerson spent some time with reporters following Day 3 of training camp practice and cleared up some rumors and give an update on his health. Dickerson said that he’s doing good, and […]
full_text: The Eagles had a lot of questions surrounding their offensive line in the months following the end of the 2025 season, but Landon Dickerson spent some time with reporters following Day 3 of training camp practice and cleared up some rumors and give an update on his health. Dickerson said that he’s doing good, and then quickly and succinctly denied reports from earlier in the offseason that he was considering retirement, noting he’s not sure where that report even came from. He also very simply replied, “Not really,” when asked if he’s got any concern about accumulating injuries over the course of his career. As for the stem cell treatment he received in Columbia this offseason — shortly after Cam Jurgens did the same —, Dickerson said that he spoke to a lot of veteran guys around the league who used the treatment, and so far, he thinks it’s helped him feel good entering training camp. He admitted that not having surgery this offseason has been nice, and shrugged off suggestions that he slimmed down at all — joking that it was no more than a big trip to the bathroom. “Not having a surgery a week before the first game — [that’s] good. Probably shouldn’t have gone out there and played, but you live and learn and you do stupid stuff when you’re young. So, I learned that mistake. Other than that, not having to get cut on is nice.” As for the lesson he learned, Dickerson pointed to not coming back before his body is ready. He also confirmed that moving forward, he’ll approach returning from injury differently, and not try to be the tough guy and push through it. “They don’t pay you to be hurt.”

full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JULY 29: Philadelphia Eagles offensive tackle Cameron Williams #73 during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on July 29th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Eagles were back on the field Saturday for their third practice of training camp , and there were several players missing — thankfully, only two were due to injuries. OT Cameron Williams suffered a knee contusion in Thursday’s practice and is still sidelined, and S Cole Wisniewski is dealing with a hamstring injury. Williams’ injury doesn’t appear to be a long-term concern, and hopefully he’s able to get back soon. Otherwise, LB Jihaad Campbell, DL Ta’Quan Graham, RT Lane Johnson , and WR Elijah Moore were all designated as “excused/not injury related.” It was a bit of a relief to see so many players missing from practice was due to other circumstances, because initial reports that Fred Johnson was in for Lane early in the day were concerning. But, ultimately, it’s a Saturday in late-summer, and they probably just had other obligations that the team deemed important enough to excuse — like Jihaad Campbell, who missed practice to to receive his degree at summer commencement from Alabama. During practice Unfortunately, there were also several injuries during practice: Rookie OLB Keyshawn James-Newby was injured during team drills and ended up being carted to the medical tent. Rookie OL Micah Morris also left practice early and was evaluated in the medical tent. Rookie OG Jaeden Roberts was unable to put any weight on his left leg after suffering an injury during the last play of the developmental period, and had to be carted inside.

summary: Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Ian Rapoport aims subtle dig towards A.J. Brown following his Philadelphia Eagles exit – HITC“Well, first of all, the no A.J. Brown is certainly different. I mean, we’ve talked about A.J. Brown as it relates to the Philadelphia Eagles for two years, and here it’s […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PA - JULY 29: Philadelphia Eagles quarterback Jalen Hurts #1 runs a drill during the Philadelphia Eagles training camp on July 29th, 2026 at Jefferson Health Training Complex in Philadelphia, PA. (Photo by Terence Lewis/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Let’s get to the Philadelphia Eagles news and links … Ian Rapoport aims subtle dig towards A.J. Brown following his Philadelphia Eagles exit – HITC “Well, first of all, the no A.J. Brown is certainly different. I mean, we’ve talked about A.J. Brown as it relates to the Philadelphia Eagles for two years, and here it’s just much quieter,” said Ian Rapoport on The Pat McAfee Show. “There’s always noise around the Eagles. In the news world, we are always going to talk about them, but it’s not the same. It’s not like, “A.J. said this today, how do you react?” It is for sure much quieter.” Jalen Carter contract: Extension details, void years, and “weight bonus” – BGN The Eagles signed Jalen Carter to a four-year extension just as training camp began. We learned that it was a $152 million deal, and now we know some more about how Howie Roseman structured things — and, you guessed it, utilized void years to cushion the cap. Roob’s Bonus Observations: Eagles thrilled with a humble, motivated Jalen Carter – NBCSP When you’re Darius Cooper and you’re undrafted and low man on the depth chart and the Eagles just added four wide receivers this offseason, you really have to find ways to stand out in limited reps. Cooper sure did that Wednesday. He made a number of good catches, most notably a diving snag of a Jalen Hurts pass down the middle of the field. What was particularly impressive was that Cooper held onto the ball after landing hard. These are the things Cooper did to make the team last year, but the WR room is deeper this year and it won’t be easy for him to stick. But if he keeps making plays like that, especially in the preseason games, he’s going to force the Eagles to make a very difficult decision. NFL’s top five defensive tackles in 2026: Jeffery Simmons at No. 1; what about Aaron Donald? – NFL.com JALEN CARTER — If this list were based solely on talent and tools, Carter would be the undisputed No. 1 player at the position. Checking in at 6-3 and 314 pounds, the No. 9 overall pick from the 2023 NFL Draft is a freak athlete with violent hands and a nasty disposition. The two-time Pro Bowler flashes “take over the game” ability when he is locked in, but his inconsistent motor and focus prevent him from dominating from the opening snap to the final whistle. That said, the steady stream of highlights makes it hard to ignore his talents as a splash-play specialist. Although he only managed to play 11 games in an erratic 2025 campaign, Carter can vault to the top of the chart if he turns it up a notch and decides he wants to dominate games week in and week out. Jalen Hurts is putting his money on Jalen Carter; Howie Roseman and the Eagles organization, even more so – PHLY Jalen Hurts’ wife put a five-dollar bill in his backpack when the Eagles’ quarterback reported for training camp Tuesday. We don’t know why – after the first workout of camp Wednesday, Hurts told reporters it was “an inside joke.” Hurts brought it up because he said he’d arrived at the team facility Tuesday, and he’d learned defensive tackle Jalen Carter had agreed to a reported four-year, $152 million contract extension, with $106 million in guarantees. “I smacked it on his chest and said, ‘Let me put a five on top of that,’” Hurts said. “He’s a great competitor, great player. He was disrupting practice out there today. I’m just excited for him to be able to focus on what’s to come.” That was the importance of general manager Howie Roseman getting Carter’s deal done before Wednesday’s first workout. Players don’t really hold out of training camp anymore, there are stiff fines for that. They do hold in, showing up but watching from the sidelines as their teammates work. That was the case Wednesday with Atlanta running back Bijan Robinson and Detroit running back Jahmyr Gibbs. The Eagles, trying to get out of the gate fresh and rested after a too-long offseason, didn’t need any of that. Carter, coming off a frustrating year marred by shoulder injuries, didn’t need any of that. After meeting a legend, ‘rare guy’ Riq Woolen is even more fired up about being an Eagle – Inquirer Riq Woolen stopped in his tracks. Following Thursday’s practice, the newest Eagles defensive back was sprinting off the field when he was waved down by one of his all-time favorite players: Hall of Famer Brian Dawkins. Woolen — who is the second tallest cornerback in the league — was enamored by the Eagles legend’s build at 52 years old. “He’s big as hell,” Woolen said with a laugh. “I didn’t expect him to be that big, bro.” People inside the building have been saying similar things about Woolen since he signed with the Eagles. Woolen, 27, is not your typical corner. Whereas other defensive backs stand at an average height of 5-foot-11 according to Joker Mag, Woolen has an impressive 6-foot-4, 210-pound frame. This physical advantage made him a Pro Bowler in 2022 and a key cog in the Seahawks’ Super Bowl run last season. These traits are the reason why general manager Howie Roseman handed him a one-year deal worth up to $15 million in March. With Woolen, Quinyon Mitchell, and Cooper DeJean in the defensive backfield, the Eagles now have three Pro Bowl cornerbacks for the first time in team history. So, how are things going with this potentially dominant trio so far? “It’s pretty cool because it’s just learning how to fit in with these guys,” Woolen said Thursday. “I know my personality, I get along well with everybody. So just being able to become close with these guys, that’s all I really care about. Jordan Mailata: If stadiums are grass for the World Cup, that should be bare minimum for us – PFT Jordan Mailata has spent his NFL career playing for the Eagles, so he’s accustomed to his home field playing surface being grass. But Mailata also just watched the World Cup get played in NFL stadiums across the nation and all of those games were also played on grass, including in places where the surface is normally turf. As a member of the NFC East, Mailata plays at MetLife Stadium and AT&T Stadium every year — two of several sites that converted to grass for the World Cup. As Philadelphia’s NFLPA rep, Mailata has added his voice to the many who are calling for all NFL games to be played on grass, particularly in light of what we all saw this summer. How the Eagles extension of Jalen Carter impacts the Seahawks – Field Gulls Williams is unquestionably in a different category than Carter or Murphy, neither of which has yet to reach their prime. At 32 years of age Williams is in the home stretch of his career, but coming off a second-team All Pro season in 2025 and back to back Pro Bowl selections, the extension Williams signs will certainly not be small, and it will undoubtedly provide another anchor point of supporting evidence towards the value of an extension for defensive linemen across the NFL, including Murphy. Further, any agent negotiating an extension for a high-level defensive lineman is all but certain to cite the recent Carter extension as evidence of a higher market for the position group as a whole, meaning that between now and whenever Murphy and the Seahawks enter contract extension talks, there will be multiple deals where the contract value was impacted by the Carter contract and then in turn used as backing for the arguments as to Murphy’s value. In short, the Carter extension resets the market for impact defensive linemen, specifically interior defensive linemen, and the Seahawks are set to extend two players to whom that description aptly applies. So, while the Carter extension won’t officially start until 2028, its impact on the league and Seattle in particular, is likely to be felt multiple times over…

title: Steelers stock report after Day Four of training camp
summary: LATROBE- After Friday’s “game practice” gave us plenty of walkthrough and offensive install notes, the helmets were back on for a well-attended Saturday practice at Saint Vincent College. It’s time to take a look at who is rising and who may be falling after the Steelers Saturday practice, and their last before pads come on […]
full_text: Jul 30, 2026; Latrobe, PA, USA; Pittsburgh Steelers linebacker Payton Wilson (left) and wide receiver DK Metcalf (4) participate in training camp drills at Saint Vincent College. Mandatory Credit: Charles LeClaire-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect LATROBE- After Friday’s “game practice” gave us plenty of walkthrough and offensive install notes, the helmets were back on for a well-attended Saturday practice at Saint Vincent College. It’s time to take a look at who is rising and who may be falling after the Steelers Saturday practice, and their last before pads come on Monday. Stock up: WR DK Metcalf Steelers star wide receiver DK Metcalf talked about how improving his communication with Aaron Rodgers was a point of emphasis this camp during his pre-training camp press conference on Tuesday. It was easy to tell the two were on the same page today. Metcalf put together what was easily his best day of camp so far. Rodgers was hitting him on all levels of the field in all areas. Metcalf made some tough catches in traffic and caught some balls where he could have picked up some serious yardage after the catch if it was a game scenario. The quarterback-receiver duo put on a show for all to see in Latrobe today. RB Lew Nichols The 2023 seventh-round pick of the Green Bay Packers has been with Pittsburgh for each of the last two training camps. Nichols had some hype after a solid preseason showing last year but was ultimately cut. Now, Nichols is back and seems to be competing for the RB3 role with the Steelers. Many have assumed that the battle would be between second-year back Kaleb Johnson and rookie seventh-round selection Eli Heidenreich, and it most likely still is, but Nichols got the majority of that work today. Nichols even ran with the first team offense in their two-minute drill to end practice. This early on in camp, teams are obviously trying lots of different things out, and Nichols was the player who benefitted the most from this today. S Robert Spears-Jennings The speedy seventh-round rookie was spotted with the starting defense opposite Jaquan Brisker to open practice. Later in practice during individual drills, Pittsburgh’s assistant head coach and secondary coach Joe Whitt Jr. was paying special attention to Spears-Jennings. Much like Nichols, Spears-Jennings benefited from the team trying out players in different situations early in camp. However, in a thinner safety room that just recruited some help today , Spears-Jennings is a name to watch when pads come on next week. Stock down: WR Germie Bernard After getting first-team reps during practice yesterday, that role seemed to go back to Roman Wilson. Near the end of practice, Mason Rudolph tried to hit a wide open Bernard over the middle that would have been a great chunk gain, but the rookie wideout was unable to haul it in. Mason Rudolph tried to hit Germie Bernard streaking across the middle but the rookie wideout dropped it. — Joey Bray (@byjoeybray) August 1, 2026 Bernard looks to be a very fluid route runner who can create separation with ease. There is still plenty of time for Bernard to separate himself from the competition and earn a starting role over the next few weeks. QB Drew Allar We are getting to see the highs and lows of the rookie third-round selection’s development in real time. I actually had thought Allar looks very solid throughout the first few days of camp accuracy wise, as well as pushing the ball down the field. To end practice today, Allar was given the opportunity to lead the offense on a two-minute drill. This drive was a perfect example of Allar both having some flashes and a lot to learn. Some of the layups, the quick underneath passes were simply off target throws by Allar. On fourth down near midfield, Allar then rifled a perfectly placed back shoulder throw to A.T. Perry over rookie cornerback Daylen Everette for a gain of about 40. Drew Allar with a 40 yard back shoulder throw to AT Perry in fourth down. Huge completion for Allar. — Joey Bray (@byjoeybray) August 1, 2026 The offense then failed to score inside the ten to end practice. While Allar made another flashy throw, it was a good reminder to everyone that he is still very much a work in progress. Let us know what you think in the comments . Today marked the final practice before the pads go on Monday, and there was plenty to discuss. Aaron Rodgers, DK Metcalf continue hot start The connection between Aaron Rodgers and DK Metcalf has been one to be excited about throughout the first week of camp. Over the last handful of days, the pair has dominated in team drills, hooking up for several completions all over the field. The crowd nearly came unglued when Rodgers launched a deep ball to Metcalf that just fell out of the receiver’s grasp after he made a diving attempt. They made up for that miss with a long completion on a crosser, as well as a deep out route. The synergy is there, and it needs to be a consistent cohesion for Pittsburgh’s offense to be more explosive in 2026. On top of his connection with Metcalf, Rodgers has just looked dialed in over this first week. He hit Roman Wilson on a deep shot over the middle for a 45-50 yard gain, and the offense won the first two-minute drill again on Saturday that ended with Rodgers throwing a bullet to Pat Freiermuth down the seam for a touchdown. He looks very comfortable and fluid within the offense, and the arm talent and vision are both still near the top of the league. Should this carry into September, this will make for a memorable swan song for the four-time MVP. Asante Samuel continues to be the best player on the field Through four practices, Asante Samuel Jr. was been the best player on either side of the ball, and he continued his hot start on Saturday. Will Howard launched a deep pass down the middle to Brandon Smith, but Samuel was there in coverage to prevent the completion. He also broke up a Rodgers pass to Metcalf during the two-minute drill. With everything going on with Joey Porter Jr, as well as the injury to Jalen Ramsey, Pittsburgh can feel good knowing Samuel is showing he is more than capable of stepping into a more prominent role. Drew Allar adds two more big time throws Drew Allar had a pair of big throws over the course of Saturday’s practice. The first came on a designed rollout to the right where he launched a pass down the right side to Kaden Wetjen for a gain of 30 yards. The second came during the second two-minute drill. On fourth down, Allar dropped back and sent a perfect back shoulder throw 40 yards down the left side of the field to A.T. Perry. The throw-and-catch set the Steelers up inside the five yard-line. And while the defense ended up holding the offense out of the end zone, the rookie continues to make notable plays. Search continues for top rotational safety To start off the day, the Steelers put rookie Robert Spears-Jennings in with the first-team defense alongside Jaquan Brisker at safety. This comes after Darnell Savage took those reps back on the first day with DeShon Elliott participating in a more limited role. Spears-Jennings possesses more sideline-to-sideline speed than any other safety on the roster, which could help him earn a spot on the 53-man roster. Pittsburgh just signed former Browns safety Rayshawn Jenkins to add to the mix, so they are leaving no stone unturned. Other notes Will Howard ripped a nice pass over the middle to Max Hurleman. His most noteworthy play of the day Jaquan Brisker blew up a jet sweep to Roman Wilson. Would have been a two-yard loss in-game T.J. Watt dropped back into coverage and picked off Aaron Rodgers. Looks like Rodgers didn’t see No. 90 lurking. Lew Nichols took reps with the first-team offense, including the entirety of the two-minute drill. Not the greatest sign for Kaleb Johnson as the Steelers continue the battle for the RB3 spot. Let us know what you think in the comments . Be sure to bookmark Behind the Steel Curtain for all the latest news, breakdowns, and more! Pittsburgh, PA 11/18/2012 CREDIT: Heinz Kluetmeier (Photo by Heinz Kluetmeier /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) (Set Number: X155803 TK1 R1 F451 ) The Pittsburgh Steelers have unveiled their 2026 Hall of Honor class Saturday, recognizing former general manager Kevin Colbert, longtime offensive lineman and broadcaster Craig Wolfley, and former cornerback J.T. We announce our Hall of Honor Class of 2026. 📺: Back Together Weekend coverage on NFL+, NFLN, and ESPN. https://t.co/FpVtLAis14 — Pittsburgh Steelers (@steelers) August 1, 2026 Colbert, who served as the Steelers’ general manager from 2000 through the 2022 NFL Draft, helped oversee one of the organization’s most successful eras. Under his leadership, Pittsburgh captured two Super Bowl championships, appeared in three Super Bowls, and consistently remained among the NFL’s perennial contenders through strong drafting and roster construction. Wolfley spent 10 seasons with the Steelers from 1980-89, earning a reputation as one of the team’s toughest offensive linemen during the decade. Following his playing career, he became a beloved voice of the franchise through his work as a Steelers radio analyst and broadcaster, further cementing his connection with the organization and its fan base. Wolfley tragically passed away on March 10 of 2025 after a long battle with cancer. Thomas starred at cornerback for the Steelers from 1973-81 and was a key member of Pittsburgh’s legendary “Steel Curtain” defense. A four-time Super Bowl champion, Thomas played a pivotal role in one of the greatest dynasties in NFL history and remains one of the standout defenders of the franchise’s championship era. The Steelers Hall of Honor celebrates individuals who have made extraordinary contributions to the organization, with the 2026 class adding three more influential figures whose impact spans the franchise’s championship success both on and off the field. The team opened the hall in 2017. Colbert, Thomas and Wolfley will be inducted at Acrisure Stadium Sept. 25.

Those are still nevertheless Kubiak ties, and while the Raiders seem set at the top of the running back depth chart with Ashton Jeanty and Mike Washington Jr, that third back is currently a battle between rookie Roman Hemby, Dylan Laube, and Chris Collier. Kubiak hasn’t brought over too many Seahawks as part of his first head coaching job. Andrew Janocko and Rick Dennison were hired over from Seattle’s coaching staff, but only Dareke Young joined the current 90-man roster , The only other ex-Seahawk even on the roster is Philip Dorsett. Maybe Kenny Mac’s next chapter will be with his most recent OC.

full_text: Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NFL. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Seahawks fans and fans across the country. Sign up here to participate in the weekly emailed surveys. Earlier in the week, fans were tasked with answering the question as to what position on the Seattle Seahawks depth chart will Jalen Milroe be placed . Obviously, it was not the starting role. That one is currently solidly in the hands of Sam Darnold, which is so nice to say. No starting quarterback controversy there. However, the question remains is whether Milroe will be the backup to Darnold, the backup to Drew Lock, or maybe not on the 53 man roster at all? The fans have answered, and here are the results! With overwhelming confidence, fans believe that Milroe will remain on the roster as QB3, with 74% of the vote. This feels right for the 2026 NFL season. While he may not be active most game days, he can be the emergency quarterback should anything happen to both Darnold and Lock on game day. I do find it fascinating how close the vote was for Milroe overtaking Lock as the backup quarterback (14%) or being off the team entirely (12%). Very stark opinions on opposite sides, but very close in the polling. Milroe does have a chance to become the backup through training camp performance and preseason play. Reports out of training camp have been positive so far for Milroe, so the next step for him will be to continue that positivity in the preseason games. As for the 12% who think Milroe will be off the team, that is unlikely for the 2026 season. I understand the logic of Darnold and Lock being similar style quarterbacks, and Milroe being a bit of an outlier and either having him on the practice squad or trading him to another team to gather more draft picks, and/or potentially another player, to free up a spot on the 53. It just does not seem like a likely option at this time for the team. What do you think? What does the future hold for Milroe? Do you agree with the results? title: Seahawks Football 101: The different types of Wide Receivers
summary: Wide receivers. They seem to come in all shapes and sizes. For awhile there the Seattle Seahawks had both DK Metcalf and Tyler Lockett, who could not be more different in terms of size and skillset. With those stark contrasts, it may make you wonder what exactly are the different kind of wide receivers? What […]
full_text: Wide receivers. They seem to come in all shapes and sizes. For awhile there the Seattle Seahawks had both DK Metcalf and Tyler Lockett, who could not be more different in terms of size and skillset. With those stark contrasts, it may make you wonder what exactly are the different kind of wide receivers? What roles do they play? That is the topic we will be tackling in today’s Football 101. Let’s get started! X-Receivers: DK Metcalf/Sidney Rice The X-receiver, also known as the split end receiver, is typically the bigger target for the quarterback outside of the tight ends. They do line up next to the tight end, and frequently on the weakside of the line close to the boundary. Oftentimes, the X-receiver is the most talented receiver on the team and is seen as WR1. They do not motion prior to the snap, and often are the biggest receivers on the team that face 1-on-1 coverage. Two past examples of X-receivers on the Seahawks are DK Metcalf and Sidney Rice. Both receivers were 6’4”, with Metcalf coming in at 230lbs and Rice at 202lbs, and both having over 33 inch arm lengths. They used their big bodies and wide wingspans to catch passes coming their way on the boundary. DK METCALF!!! SEAHAWKS TOUCHDOWN pic.twitter.com/RAgxydWPcB — Seattle ON Tap (@SeattleONTap) December 26, 2021 Y-Receivers: Doug Baldwin/Jaxon Smith-Njigba The Y-receiver, or the slot receiver, is a player who takes on the role a tight end generally would, or in some cases are the tight end. They line up next to the offensive tackle and on run plays will often assist in run blocking, but on pass plays will run short-to-intermediate routes like drags, slants, seams, as well as option routes with the goal of taking advantage of linebackers and safeties. Both Doug Baldwin and Jaxon Smith-Njigba have played this role perfectly. Though both have lined up in different receiving roles, the Y-receiver is their bread and butter. Smith-Njigba can be seen as the X-receiver at times for the current iteration of the team; when the wide receiver trio was Lockett, Metcalf and Smith-Njigba, he was typically the Y-receiver. & well, I had to add this one, it might be more of a Russell Wilson video, but Doug Baldwin OF COURSE, was the man behind the catch. One of the most wild plays ever. pic.twitter.com/ni0N2NcSbR — Sami ON Tap (@SamiOnTap) November 16, 2023 Z-Receivers: Steve Largent/Tyler Lockett Z-receivers, or flankers, are typically the speedsters, but not always. They line up off the line of scrimmage and can beat out any initial attempt to jam them within the first five yards of a route. Flankers do often get lined up outside like X-receivers but can be flexed out when needed. Steve Largent and Tyler Lockett both have played the role of Z-receiver, using motion, precision route running, and football speed to get open and create yards after the catch. Largent was especially a master of route running, always finding a way to get open, and held many receiving records for the NFL as he went on his way to the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Nobody looked better in those @Seahawks throwbacks than Steve Largent 🔥 pic.twitter.com/GofUJMnYuL — NFL Films (@NFLFilms) June 6, 2023 Oh my goodness, Tyler Lockett! How did Russell Wilson fit that in? Insane throw. Incredible catch. Wowww pic.twitter.com/5o1GwW0hru — Ari Meirov (@MySportsUpdate) October 4, 2019 Receiver is such a multi-faceted role on the team. They may line up as either X, Y or Z for one play, but can change up their positioning for the next play to keep the opposing defense guessing. Smith-Njigba did that last year for the Seahawks. Tell me, though, who is your favorite receiver you’ve watched play for the Seahawks? Who is your current favorite receiver on the team? Who do you think will have a break out season in 2026? title: 49ers injuries: De’Zhaun Stribling has hamstring tightness; Keion White has an adductor issue
summary: The San Francisco 49ers headed into Saturday’s practice thin at wide receiver. Ricky Pearsall’s season is over with a lingering PCL injury. Christian Kirk has a calf strain. According to the media on hand, rookie wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling isn’t practicing due to hamstring tightness. This team cannot catch a break. There’s no need for […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - MAY 28: De'Zhaun Stribling #15 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during a team OTA practice at SAP Performance Facility on May 28, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images The San Francisco 49ers headed into Saturday’s practice thin at wide receiver. Ricky Pearsall’s season is over with a lingering PCL injury. Christian Kirk has a calf strain . According to the media on hand, rookie wide receiver De’Zhaun Stribling isn’t practicing due to hamstring tightness. This team cannot catch a break. There’s no need for the Niners to push Stribling, so if there’s any indication of tightness or injury, they should give their first-year wideout as much time as he needs to return 100%. The 49ers want to avoid it becoming a strain. The more the top wideouts miss, the more other players will get their opportunities. We know about Jordan Watkins and Jacob Cowing, but undrafted free agent Wesley Grimes is a big beneficiary, as he could potentially slide into the “F” role, being a bigger body, as well as “Z” opposite Mike Evans. Grimes was our sleeper pick to push for a roster spot, but make the practice squad at the very least. UDFA rookie pass rusher Mikail Kamara was carted off Rookie undrafted free agent pass rusher Mikail Kamara was carted off the practice field with an apparent leg/knee issue, per The Athletic’s Matt Barrows. The team was already missing Cam Sample with a knee injury. Edge rusher is another position the 49ers can’t afford to be without bodies, as Nick Bosa still hasn’t practiced and Mykel Williams is on the PUP list. We don’t want to assume the worst for Kamara. His injury history is suboptimal. Kamara suffered season-ending injuries that caused him to miss the 2021 and 2022 seasons in college. Kamara has had a torn labrum and multiple high-ankle sprains at James Madison. Keion White’s injury Keion White and Romello Height were also absent from Saturday’s session. Height was recently carted off, although the time clarified that it was just cramps. White sat out with an adductor issue. White has had minor injuries during his career. This wouldn’t be the first time he’s dealt with a groin injury, though. He was listed on the Patriots injury report multiple times in 2024 with groin designations. The slew of injuries at defensive end meant the 49ers only had two players, Sam Okuayinonu and KJ Henry, as healthy bodies to practice. Kevin Givens, a defensive tackle, had to play snaps along the edge.

summary: San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch said that the team is placing wide receiver Ricky Pearsall on the season-ending Injured Reserve. Pearsall will have surgery on his PCL, and the recovery time is anywhere from 6 to 12 months. As Matt Maiocco pointed out a couple of days ago, the 49ers were hopeful that […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - JULY 27: Ricky Pearsall #1 of the San Francisco 49ers works out during training camp practice at SAP Performance Facility on July 27, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images San Francisco 49ers general manager John Lynch said that the team is placing wide receiver Ricky Pearsall on the season-ending Injured Reserve. Pearsall will have surgery on his PCL, and the recovery time is anywhere from 6 to 12 months. As Matt Maiocco pointed out a couple of days ago, the 49ers were hopeful that Pearsall’s PCL injury would heal on its own. Unfortunately, it only took a few practices for the team to realize that wasn’t the case. It would have been a nagging injury throughout the season, leaving the team no choice but to pull the plug on the 2026 season. Pearsall is expected to recover in time for the 2027 season. The good news is that Pearsall turns 26 in September and has plenty of football left. The bad news is he has suffered some type of injury that will now have sidelined him in each of his first three seasons. Pearsall, a former 1st-round pick, was incredible for the first month of 2025. But that PCL injury clearly zapped some of the juice he had, as he didn’t have another 100-yard game in the final five games he played in. The corresponding move was to sign Deebo Samuel to a one-year deal officially. There are still no specifics about the incentives in Samuel’s contract. Lynch said the team had been in contact with Samuel for about a month. The 49ers were hoping Deebo and Pearsall would be on the field together, but now a role opens for Samuel.

That’s another name who could help take on some of Marathe’s duties if Hampton doesn’t fill every role.

title: Adam Schefter: 49ers, Deebo Samuel have been talking for weeks
summary: With Ricky Pearsall’s 2026 uncertain, the 49ers needed to prepare for the worst, and Deebo Samuel being signed Thursday was that preparation. According to Adam Schefter, it wasn’t so much of a knee-jerk reaction to Pearsall’s PCL injury as it may appear. Appearing on the Pat McAfee show, Schefter broke down what led to Samuel’s […]
full_text: San Francisco 49ers' Ricky Pearsall and Deebo Samuel walk off the field after Detroit Lions' 40-34 win in NFL game at Levi's Stadium in Santa Clara, Calif., on Monday, December 30, 2024. (Photo by Scott Strazzante/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images) With Ricky Pearsall’s 2026 uncertain , the 49ers needed to prepare for the worst, and Deebo Samuel being signed Thursday was that preparation. According to Adam Schefter, it wasn’t so much of a knee-jerk reaction to Pearsall’s PCL injury as it may appear. Appearing on the Pat McAfee show , Schefter broke down what led to Samuel’s signing and how it wasn’t just a few days of talk. “The truth of the matter is Deebo had been talking to the 49ers all along, and the 49ers had told him that they were interested in bringing him back to San Francisco for weeks. There were actual conversations that occurred between Kyle Shanahan and Deebo Samuel. I think Deebo obviously was looking to see what kind of deal he could land on the open market, and when those deals that he was looking for don’t materialize, and those conversations with San Francisco continue on, and all of a sudden there are questions about Ricky Pearsall—who by the way right now is continuing to meet with doctors—he’s got another meeting planned for Monday right now with another doctor, but he’s going through his meetings with doctors and there are absolute questions about if and when he’ll be able to play this season that have to be answered still by the doctors. The Niners have been talking to Deebo. No other offers had materialized—meaningful offers. And so in the end, we’ve seen what San Francisco can do with Deebo, how the 49ers utilize him. He’s dangerous in their offense and I would imagine will be a factor again this year.” This adds up to all the social media fun the 49ers were having with Samuel. Fullback Kyle Juszczyk and tight end George Kittle entered a bidding war , offering their summer homes as a place for Samuel to stay. It sounds like Deebo and the 49ers reuniting was more expedited with the Pearsall injury rather than being an immediate fix. Given that he was looking for what he could make on the open market, had Pearsall not gone down, the 49ers may have rolled the dice and waited until mid-season for a player to go down before bringing Samuel in (similar to how Kendrick Bourne came to the team last year). Obviously that has its own challenges, namely keeping Samuel from signing elsewhere, but before Pearsall’s knee flared up, it was harder to justify a roster spot with what the 49ers had. This will give their first pick in the 2026 NFL Draft, second-rounder De’Zhaun Stribling, even more veteran tutelage along with Mike Evans.

title: Ricky Pearsall waiting to have surgery on PCL wasn’t avoidance; it was medically sound
summary: Ricky Pearsall is currently out of the San Francisco 49ers’ training camp with a PCL injury, and initial reports say he might be out for much longer than that. While it did give us the return of Deebo Samuel to fill the wide receiver spot in an extended Pearsall absence, it’s rather concerning for Pearsall, […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WA - JANUARY 17: Ricky Pearsall #1 of the San Francisco 49ers in the locker room before the NFC Divisional Playoff game against the Seattle Seahawks at Lumen Field on January 17, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. The Seahawks defeated the 49ers 41-6. (Photo by Michael Zagaris/San Francisco 49ers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ricky Pearsall is currently out of the San Francisco 49ers’ training camp with a P CL injury, and initial reports say he might be out for much longer than that. While it did give us the return of Deebo Samuel to fill the wide receiver spot in an extended Pearsall absence, it’s rather concerning for Pearsall, a player who had little issue in college dealing with injuries, getting another season derailed due to an injury. This injury was re-aggravated in December of 2025 , and so now, in 2026 training camp, the wide receiver is going to be considering surgery? As you might expect, this has some fans questioning the timing. Why did he wait until 49ers training camp when symptoms showed up to now be considering an operation when he could have done it during the offseason? Oh the timing! Oh the bad medical advice! Oh, that’s actually what doctors recommend. On X, Dr. Nirav Pandya went over why these cases usually avoid surgery until it’s a last resort: Re: PCL injuries and the Rickey Pearsall situation. In general, the vast majority of PCL injuries are managed non-operatively; especially if they are isolated. If patients become symptomatic (swelling, pain, or instability), then surgery can be performed. Sometimes the symptoms… — Dr. Nirav Pandya, M.D. (@DrNiravPandya) July 29, 2026 The post has that “show more” button, so here’s what else was said in the same post regarding surgery: Sometimes the symptoms won’t creep up until players really start doing intensive activities. The reason to try and delay PCL surgery is that reconstruction has a long recovery process (9-12 months) and results are mixed; especially at an agility position like WR. The word is ‘mixed results’. Not every player returns from a surgery the same way they were before. Sure, the 49ers and Pearsall could have decided surgery was the best option last year, but then they open up a whole new mess of potential problems. While Pearsall’s future in the NFL may be uncertain, the surgery would add another wrinkle to the uncertainty. What I’m getting at is it wasn’t some ill-advised decision to leave surgery until absolutely necessary and avoiding surgery wasn’t an option Pearsall or the 49ers were going for—it’s generally what is recommended. Pearsall practiced, then symptoms appeared during training camp. These are not paper cuts; they take months to heal on their own without surgery. There’s nothing Pearsall could have done differently, according to many medical professionals. Now it might be time for the last resort. “The data on these is not good surgically,” Dr. Jesse Morse said on X when discussing the injury. So basically, rehab and rest are the first steps to recovery from this injury. Going under the knife is a last resort due to the risks and complications. Surgery still isn’t official either; it’s just an option and something discussed. An “if” of sorts. The first step was to see if this would heal on its own. It clearly is not after a generous amount of time, so now they look at other alternatives. Hopefully, with a few more weeks or months, this goes away for good.

title: Do Styles, Chenal & Luvu hold the key to Washington’s success in 2026?
summary: Competition, competition, competition Dan Quinn has been adamant this will be the Commanders’ most competitive training camp since he took over in 2024. “You’ll find some competition in an everyday sense, and I think that’s one of the very best ways that we’ll get better — just good-on-good situations. Into tomorrow, there’ll be a two-point […]
full_text: Competition, competition, competition Dan Quinn has been adamant this will be the Commanders’ most competitive training camp since he took over in 2024. “You’ll find some competition in an everyday sense, and I think that’s one of the very best ways that we’ll get better — just good-on-good situations. Into tomorrow, there’ll be a two-point play competition — best out of five — and those are the moments I think you’ll find some game scenarios and situations in every practice [like] two minute and four minute [drills], last plays, setting up field goals. “Can we put ourselves in these spots so when we the air gets thin, that we feel like that’s our space, and we’re going to work really hard into that spot? I feel a hunger from the team, so they’re ready to get into that.” Reacts survey This week’s Reacts survey comprised a single question: Outside of quarterback, which position group’s development during this training camp will most dictate the Commanders’ success in the 2026 season? The results were a bit unusual in that four different position groups got double-digit percentages of the overall vote. Visit our partners at FanDuel Two defensive groups (LBs and DBs) and two offensive groups (WR/TEs and OL) comprised those 4 groups of top vote-getters. In my mind, the four groups break out into three sub-groups when it comes to why readers voted for them. Group 1: High confidence The linebacking corps drew the largest percentage of this week’s responses, and I believe that’s because fans feel highly confident that this is a deep and talented position group. In fact, I’ve heard and read many people (myself included) suggest that this is the best overall group of inside linebackers that the Commanders has fielded in recent memory. It may take some time to adjust to thinking about Washington’s edge rushers as primarily aligning as outside linebackers in a 3-man front instead of DEs in a 4-man front, but the work that Adam Peters did this offseason to re-make the edge rushing group was also part of what drove some Hogs Haven readers to vote for this position group. To put a finer point on it, I think these 12 players are the ones that likely are in most people’s minds when they think of Washington’s training camp linebackers: Anchoring the middle, the inside linebackers appear to bring elite instincts, lateral speed, and bone-crushing physicality. While Sonny Styles is a rookie and unproven at the pro level, he is the son of an NFL player, and was drafted 7 th overall for a number of good reasons. Expectations are high that Styles will step right into a high-performance group, and that the rookie will see a lot of play time alongside proven veterans Leo Chenal and Frankie Luvu. Frankie, in 2025, was asked to play out of position for much of the season to make up for a devastating number of injuries to other players. With him back in his natural position and in a scheme that is built to take advantage of his strengths, the group’s sideline-to-sideline pursuit ought to be perfectly complemented by the still-developing high-motor play of Jordan Magee, with Kain Medrano, and Ale Kaho competing for roster spots primarily on the strength of their special teams play. On the perimeter, the outside linebackers have gotten a lot of “wows” from training camp observers in the first two days. With their size and experience, they should provide a terrifying edge presence characterized by raw speed and versatile coverage capabilities. The explosive tandem of Odafe Oweh and Dorance Armstrong will likely have the ability to set a ferocious edge against the run while consistently collapsing the pocket. Complemented by the twitchy athleticism of K’Lavon Chaisson and the length and potential of rookie Joshua Josephs, this group will be counted on to create consistent pressure, made relentless by the expected blitz-heavy scheme of new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. Both Javonte Jean-Baptiste, who played about 26% of defensive snaps over the past two seasons, and Drake Jackson, who appeared in the final 3 games of the ’25 season after being activated from injured reserve, look to be on the roster bubble in 2026 following March and April roster upgrades. Group 2: Shaky confidence The pass catchers and defensive backs each drew about 1 in 5 voters this week, and I think the reason was that many Commanders fans remain unconvinced that Washington’s front office did enough to ensure that the starting talent is good enough or that the depth is sufficient to withstand injuries to starters. Pass catchers For the purposes of the survey, I had to combine the WRs and TEs together. At tight end, I think most fans are sold on Chig Okonkwo being an explosive playmaker in the passing game, but may have more questions about his run game blocking. John Bates would be his mirror image as a skilled blocker, but merely a competent receiver. Questions hover around 2024 second-round pick Ben Sinnott, as well as 2024 UDFA Colson Yankoff. The bigger concerns at WR have been discussed all offseason. Firstly , does Washington have enough skill at the position outside of Terry McLaurin, with the rookie Antonio Williams being added to the group of veterans that all have question marks: Luke McCaffrey, Jaylin Lane, Dyami Brown, Treylon Burks and Van Jefferson? "If Jayden Daniels is sitting back there and nobody's getting open with a decent scheme, that puts him into a position where he's at more risk because he's extending and he's running more." – Kevin Sheehan on the risk of Commanders' lack of WR depth pic.twitter.com/wfu4pGsVXj — The Team 980 (@team980) July 31, 2026 Many argue that, if Jayden Daniels is healthy, he will elevate this group of generally undistinguished receivers to achieve on the field just like he did in 2024. In fact, the argument can be made that: (a) this group is more skilled than the ‘24 group was; (b) Daniels is a more fully developed QB than he was in ‘24; and (c) the new offensive coordinator will be better able to use scheme and motion to create passing opportunities than was true in ‘24. So, maybe, with a healthy JD5, this group will be good enough. That raises the second concern , however, of whether the group can perform at a playoff level if Terry McLaurin misses significant playing time , as he did in 2025. His absence from the field in training camp and most of the regular season last year is seen by many as a central factor in the team’s struggles. His presence throughout the offseason so far in 2026 has been credited as a major factor in a more energetic ‘vibe’ in this year’s camp. It’s hard to overstate the negative impact that another serious injury to Terry would have on the 2026 season, making the lack of a clear playmaking #2 receiver an issue that simply won’t go away. One noticeable difference at #Commanders camp this year is Terry McLaurin The difference? He's there… and practicing! With last year's contract dispute in the rear view, the star WR has his focus on performing, and mentoring. @JPFinlayNBCS has the story #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/V7C5w704bG — NBC4 Sports (@NBC4Sports) July 31, 2026 Defensive backs The concerns about the DBs mirror those that surround the wide receivers. There are no proven stars at safety or cornerback, and question marks are linked to health, size, or performance of nearly every player in the position group. While many people have made strong arguments that Nick Cross, Will Harris, Trey Amos, Mikey Sainristil, Amik Robertson or Rasul Douglas will play very well this year in Daronte Jones’ expected new blitz-heavy, zone-heavy scheme, a different fan, analyst or observer could make an equally strong evidence-backed case against each of those players having a great year in 2026. Clearly, as defined in this week’s question, the development of the secondary during this training camp will probably have a lot to do with the Commanders’ success in the coming season. full_text: Daron Payne isn’t the longest-tenured Commanders player. Punter Tress Way holds that title. Still, the defensive tackle has been around the block a few times now, entering his ninth season in Washington . The Alabama product has seen some things during that time. He has been to the playoffs twice , including 2024’s deep postseason run. Results, however, have largely been unpleasant. Payne has experienced just one winning season (in 2024) since being selected No. 13 overall in the 2018 NFL draft. Payne has worked with four defensive coordinators and five defensive play callers heading into this season, with Daronte Jones now taking control. As someone who has been to the puppet show and seen the strings, we can trust Payne when he says something feels different in the best possible way. That’s how he’s describing Jones’ new defensive system. “When we’re in defensive meetings, I just listen to the way he explains it,” Payne said in a press conference after Saturday’s practice. “He’s like a mad scientist, the way he explains how to disguise and the things for the DBs, but it’s cool to see. It’s much harder than what the D-line got to do. I can say that.” The defensive line won’t remain static. That intrigues Payne, the ability to move around some, find advantageous matchups and showcase some versatility. “I just feel like I’m just being more versatile. … I get to play outside, I get to play inside,” Payne said. “It’s not like I just stay in one spot. I can play all along the line.” Look, Payne isn’t rushing off the edge. The 6-foot-3, 320-pound lineman can work all three defensive line spots, though, from various techniques. Payne’s able to do that because the Commanders have some big dudes up front. The defensive line contains six guys above 300 pounds and four above 315, including three presumptively involved in the regular-season rotation. “We got [DT Javon] Kinlaw, [DT Tim] Settle, [DT Jer’Zhan] Newton, a bunch of just big, strong guys that are not just big and strong, but they can also move, too,” Payne said. “So, it’s just fun being able to play with guys and we don’t have to just be stuck in one position. We can all just move, move along.” Having such heft means Payne isn’t stuck in the middle and could uncork some of the pass-rush ability that has shown up at various points in his career (though not lately). Run defense and block absorption is going to be important in the Commanders base three-man front. Payne’s in the last year of his deal, certainly hunting for an elusive third big NFL contract. He was at his best during his last contract year, so there’s hope he’ll be highly motivated and productive. If this is in fact Payne’s final season in Washington – his 2026 production and his open market value will likely define that – a strong finish is wanted. “Man, it’s a blessing to be in one place for so long in the NFL,” Payne said. “Guys don’t really stay in one place a long time, so this is a blessing to be here. I just want to be here to help get to where we want to go.”

full_text: The Washington Commanders are back on the practice fields after having a light walk through day yesterday with no media. The fans were in attendance for the first time on Saturday, and it should be a great opportunity for them to see the new team in action. Head coach Dan Quinn stepped up to the microphone before practice to answer questions from the media on the third day of training camp. Quinn gave some injury updates to open up his Saturday morning presser. Tight end John Bates is dealing with a hamstring injury that will keep him out for a few weeks. This injury is unfortunate for the offense as Bates is the best blocker at the position, but it will give other players opportunities to get reps during camp. Nick Allegretti missed Day 2 with a calf strain, and he’s probably going to miss another week, giving veteran Julian Good-Jones and rookie Matt Gulbin more reps. Quinn also provided a positive injury updates. WR Treylon Burks sat out practice on Thursday due to some soreness in his foot, but he’s back on the field today. full_text: The Daily Slop – 1 AUGUST 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links Articles Bullock’s Film Room (this very detailed article can be read for free in its entirety) How NFL Training Camp Installs Work Obviously, I don’t have David Blough’s playbook and camp installs as he’s a first time offensive coordinator and has only just put them together. But I do have some other examples to give you a good idea of what exactly is going on inside the building. Different teams will do things differently but generally teams will go about things in one of two ways. Some teams prefer to have meetings and install sessions in the morning, then take those teachings out to the field for practice in the afternoon, before reviewing the film in the evening. It’s a nice way of having a clear blocked out day for each install session. Other teams will do things slightly differently. They might prefer to have the install meetings in the evening, giving players something to study at home in the evening and test their retention at practice the following morning. Then after practice they’ll review the film in the afternoon before moving onto the next install session in the evening. Both are valid options. I believe Dan Quinn typically prefers the latter option with install meetings at night and practice first thing in the morning Most offenses will break up their playbook into 10-14 install days, depending on the volume of plays they have in the playbook. On day one, they will be installing their core fundamental plays and then, if the coordinator is organized and well structured, they will add layers to those day one concepts in the following days to build out the offense. So what does this look like exactly? Well, here’s an example from Kyle Shanahan’s 2018 training camp install with the San Francisco 49ers. View Link There are lots of situational football things that come up at camp too. Dan Quinn in particular loves to allocate time for specific situations like red zone or two minute drills. Those will be different parts of the playbook but installed in the same way. Most teams will have about 12 days of installing their offense like this, building up layers and layers for their players each day. A trend I’ve seen more recently is that many teams will often reset back to day one of installs midway through training camp. Camp lasts a lot longer than just 12 days, so resetting halfway through to ensure everything is fully installed and the finer details are understood is a good way to go about things. Not every team will do that though. Dan Quinn said in his press conference yesterday they had already been through the installs once during OTAs and mini camp, so that will certainly help. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Hogs Haven Does WAS have a SB Offense? If you look at WRs only, the WAS crew comes up very short unless you are projecting historic performance improvements from several of them and unless Antonio Williams delivers the performance of the first rounder that NFL scouts once thought he was. However, if you look at the top 3 receivers at any position on SB teams, it’s a different story. It turns out 13 of the last 20 SB teams have a TE or a RB as one of their top 3 receivers, and 4 of those teams had the combination of WR, TE, and RB in the top 3 receiving positions. WAS doesn’t look so bad seen in that light. McLaurin locks down the WR position. Onkonkwo is below but not that far from #2 averages, 56 receptions for 560 yards versus 68 for 877 for the average #2 on a SB team. It’s not hard to imagine that he can produce more with Daniels than he did with Cam Ward. White is almost exactly at the #3 average for receptions (his career average is 52, versus 51 for the average #3 receiver on a SB team). However, his yardage is on the light side at 368 versus an average #3 of 595. This is not a new problem for White. He has always had a low yards / reception number even for a running back. But he makes a credible #3 option. Although Okonkwo and White are not elite receivers, they are good and they are better than those on some teams that won the SB. I was surprised at how often SB teams had only one elite receiving option – or none, in a few cases. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Hail Mail | Camp stars and early rookie thoughts I know it’s early but who has impressed you so far in camp? I was very impressed with what I saw from Treylon Burks on the first day of camp. I know he’s dealing with some foot soreness that forced him to miss Thursday’s practice, but he did several things that could help answer some questions the fans have about the wide receivers behind Terry McLaurin. As for the foot soreness, I know fans are going to feel uneasy about it, considering his injury history with the Tennessee Titans. I can empathize with those feelings, but foot soreness is not the same as a sprain or a soft tissue injury, so let’s take Quinn for his word that it’s not overly concerning and see how camp progresses before making any conclusions. Heard defense is faster this year, how has the offense adapted? I think the offense is in the process of finding that adaptation that you’re looking for. From a straight-up execution standpoint, I feel like both sides of the ball have been relatively equal, although the defense did perform better on Thursday than Wednesday. But it does take some time to truly get a feel for what a defense is trying to do to you. Eventually, the ball will come out quicker at a more consistent rate. The offensive line will work together to counter the pass rush’s speed. So, just to answer your question succinctly, the offense is in the process of matching the defense’s speed and is making progress there. Also, keep in mind that defenses tend to look better when the pads aren’t on because of the restrictions on contact. I think we’ll have a better idea of where the units stack up when the pads come on next week. What it does tell us is that Washington is interested, but appears to be trying to let it play out with the guys already in their building. Keim would not tweet that for any other reason. Washington could continue to evaluate their talent in the receiver room for the rest of camp without completely closing the door on adding another proven veteran. title: With DQ’s focus on competition, Commanders must gel as a team to win
summary: Competition, competition, competition Dan Quinn has been adamant this will be the Commanders’ most competitive training camp since he took over in 2024. “You’ll find some competition in an everyday sense, and I think that’s one of the very best ways that we’ll get better — just good-on-good situations. Into tomorrow, there’ll be a two-point […]
full_text: Competition, competition, competition Dan Quinn has been adamant this will be the Commanders’ most competitive training camp since he took over in 2024. “You’ll find some competition in an everyday sense, and I think that’s one of the very best ways that we’ll get better — just good-on-good situations. Into tomorrow, there’ll be a two-point play competition — best out of five — and those are the moments I think you’ll find some game scenarios and situations in every practice [like] two minute and four minute [drills], last plays, setting up field goals. “Can we put ourselves in these spots so when we the air gets thin, that we feel like that’s our space, and we’re going to work really hard into that spot? I feel a hunger from the team, so they’re ready to get into that.” Reacts survey This week’s Reacts survey comprised a single question: Outside of quarterback, which position group’s development during this training camp will most dictate the Commanders’ success in the 2026 season? The results were a bit unusual in that four different position groups got double-digit percentages of the overall vote. Visit our partners at FanDuel Two defensive groups (LBs and DBs) and two offensive groups (WR/TEs and OL) comprised those 4 groups of top vote-getters. In my mind, the four groups break out into three sub-groups when it comes to why readers voted for them. Group 1: High confidence The linebacking corps drew the largest percentage of this week’s responses, and I believe that’s because fans feel highly confident that this is a deep and talented position group. In fact, I’ve heard and read many people (myself included) suggest that this is the best overall group of inside linebackers that the Commanders has fielded in recent memory. It may take some time to adjust to thinking about Washington’s edge rushers as primarily aligning as outside linebackers in a 3-man front instead of DEs in a 4-man front, but the work that Adam Peters did this offseason to re-make the edge rushing group was also part of what drove some Hogs Haven readers to vote for this position group. To put a finer point on it, I think these 12 players are the ones that likely are in most people’s minds when they think of Washington’s training camp linebackers: Anchoring the middle, the inside linebackers appear to bring elite instincts, lateral speed, and bone-crushing physicality. While Sonny Styles is a rookie and unproven at the pro level, he is the son of an NFL player, and was drafted 7 th overall for a number of good reasons. Expectations are high that Styles will step right into a high-performance group, and that the rookie will see a lot of play time alongside proven veterans Leo Chenal and Frankie Luvu. Frankie, in 2025, was asked to play out of position for much of the season to make up for a devastating number of injuries to other players. With him back in his natural position and in a scheme that is built to take advantage of his strengths, the group’s sideline-to-sideline pursuit ought to be perfectly complemented by the still-developing high-motor play of Jordan Magee, with Kain Medrano, and Ale Kaho competing for roster spots primarily on the strength of their special teams play. On the perimeter, the outside linebackers have gotten a lot of “wows” from training camp observers in the first two days. With their size and experience, they should provide a terrifying edge presence characterized by raw speed and versatile coverage capabilities. The explosive tandem of Odafe Oweh and Dorance Armstrong will likely have the ability to set a ferocious edge against the run while consistently collapsing the pocket. Complemented by the twitchy athleticism of K’Lavon Chaisson and the length and potential of rookie Joshua Josephs, this group will be counted on to create consistent pressure, made relentless by the expected blitz-heavy scheme of new defensive coordinator Daronte Jones. Both Javonte Jean-Baptiste, who played about 26% of defensive snaps over the past two seasons, and Drake Jackson, who appeared in the final 3 games of the ’25 season after being activated from injured reserve, look to be on the roster bubble in 2026 following March and April roster upgrades. Group 2: Shaky confidence The pass catchers and defensive backs each drew about 1 in 5 voters this week, and I think the reason was that many Commanders fans remain unconvinced that Washington’s front office did enough to ensure that the starting talent is good enough or that the depth is sufficient to withstand injuries to starters. Pass catchers For the purposes of the survey, I had to combine the WRs and TEs together. At tight end, I think most fans are sold on Chig Okonkwo being an explosive playmaker in the passing game, but may have more questions about his run game blocking. John Bates would be his mirror image as a skilled blocker, but merely a competent receiver. Questions hover around 2024 second-round pick Ben Sinnott, as well as 2024 UDFA Colson Yankoff. The bigger concerns at WR have been discussed all offseason. Firstly , does Washington have enough skill at the position outside of Terry McLaurin, with the rookie Antonio Williams being added to the group of veterans that all have question marks: Luke McCaffrey, Jaylin Lane, Dyami Brown, Treylon Burks and Van Jefferson? "If Jayden Daniels is sitting back there and nobody's getting open with a decent scheme, that puts him into a position where he's at more risk because he's extending and he's running more." – Kevin Sheehan on the risk of Commanders' lack of WR depth pic.twitter.com/wfu4pGsVXj — The Team 980 (@team980) July 31, 2026 Many argue that, if Jayden Daniels is healthy, he will elevate this group of generally undistinguished receivers to achieve on the field just like he did in 2024. In fact, the argument can be made that: (a) this group is more skilled than the ‘24 group was; (b) Daniels is a more fully developed QB than he was in ‘24; and (c) the new offensive coordinator will be better able to use scheme and motion to create passing opportunities than was true in ‘24. So, maybe, with a healthy JD5, this group will be good enough. That raises the second concern , however, of whether the group can perform at a playoff level if Terry McLaurin misses significant playing time , as he did in 2025. His absence from the field in training camp and most of the regular season last year is seen by many as a central factor in the team’s struggles. His presence throughout the offseason so far in 2026 has been credited as a major factor in a more energetic ‘vibe’ in this year’s camp. It’s hard to overstate the negative impact that another serious injury to Terry would have on the 2026 season, making the lack of a clear playmaking #2 receiver an issue that simply won’t go away. One noticeable difference at #Commanders camp this year is Terry McLaurin The difference? He's there… and practicing! With last year's contract dispute in the rear view, the star WR has his focus on performing, and mentoring. @JPFinlayNBCS has the story #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/V7C5w704bG — NBC4 Sports (@NBC4Sports) July 31, 2026 Defensive backs The concerns about the DBs mirror those that surround the wide receivers. There are no proven stars at safety or cornerback, and question marks are linked to health, size, or performance of nearly every player in the position group. While many people have made strong arguments that Nick Cross, Will Harris, Trey Amos, Mikey Sainristil, Amik Robertson or Rasul Douglas will play very well this year in Daronte Jones’ expected new blitz-heavy, zone-heavy scheme, a different fan, analyst or observer could make an equally strong evidence-backed case against each of those players having a great year in 2026. Clearly, as defined in this week’s question, the development of the secondary during this training camp will probably have a lot to do with the Commanders’ success in the coming season.
